label: def:g-permutable
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:g-permutable}
Let $A\leq G$. We say that $A$ is \emph{$G$-permutable} in $G$ if for every subgroup $B\leq G$ there is an element $x\in G$ with
$$
        AB^x=B^xA.
$$
We say that $A$ is \emph{hereditarily $G$-permutable} in $G$ if $A$ is $E$-permutable in $E$ for every subgroup $E$ with $A\leq E\leq G$. These definitions follow Skiba \cite[Definitions 2.1 and 2.2]{Skiba2006}.
head: environment

label: conj:gt
title: Conjecture
body_md:
\label{conj:gt}
A nontrivial finite group $G$ is simple if and only if $G$ has no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

label: thm:main
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:main}
No nonabelian finite simple group $G$ has a proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

label: cor:simplicity-criterion
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{cor:simplicity-criterion}
A nontrivial finite group $G$ is simple if and only if $G$ has no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If $G$ is not simple, then $G$ has a proper nontrivial normal subgroup $N$. For every subgroup $B\leq G$ the product $NB=BN$ is again a subgroup, and the equality $NB=BN$ holds inside every subgroup $E$ with $N\leq E\leq G$ because $N\unlhd E$. Hence $N$ is a proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup. Conversely, suppose that $G$ is simple. If $G$ is abelian, then $G$ is cyclic of prime order and has no proper nontrivial subgroup at all. If $G$ is nonabelian, then we use Theorem \ref{thm:main}. In each case $G$ has no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

label: lem:generated-hereditary-formulation
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:generated-hereditary-formulation}
For $A\leq G$, the hereditary condition of {\rm Definition \ref{def:g-permutable}} is equivalent to the following: for every subgroup $B\leq G$ there exists $x\in \langle A,B\rangle$ with $AB^x=B^xA$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Suppose that $A$ is hereditarily $G$-permutable. For $B\leq G$, we use hereditary permutability of $A$ inside $E=\langle A,B\rangle$. Consequently, the conjugating element provided by this hereditary permutability condition lies in $\langle A,B\rangle$. Conversely, suppose that the condition in the lemma holds, and let $A\leq E\leq G$ with $B\leq E$. The conjugating element $x$ for $A$ and $B$ lies in $\langle A,B\rangle\leq E$ and shows that $A$ permutes with $B^x$ inside $E$.
head: environment

label: lem:maximal-product
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:maximal-product}
Let $A\leq G$ be hereditarily $G$-permutable and let $M\leq G$. Then there is $x\in \langle A,M\rangle$ for which $AM^x$ is a subgroup of $G$. If moreover $M$ is maximal in $G$, then either $A\leq M^x$ or $G=AM^x$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: By hereditary $G$-permutability of $A$ for $M$, we have $x\in\langle A,M\rangle$ with $AM^x=M^xA$, so $AM^x$ is a subgroup. If $M$ is maximal, then $AM^x$, which contains $M^x$, equals $M^x$ or $G$.
head: environment

label: lem:ordinary-maximal-product
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:ordinary-maximal-product}
Let $A\leq G$ be ordinarily $G$-permutable and let $M\leq G$. Then there is $x\in G$ for which $AM^x$ is a subgroup of $G$. If $M$ is maximal in $G$, then either $A\leq M^x$ or $G=AM^x$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We repeat the argument of Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product}, with $x\in G$ chosen by ordinary $G$-permutability of $A$.
head: environment

label: lem:factorization-coset-transitivity
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:factorization-coset-transitivity}
Let $G$ act on the right cosets of a subgroup $M$ by right multiplication. For $A\leq G$, the group $A$ is transitive on the right cosets of $M$ in $G$ if and only if $G=MA=AM$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The $A$-orbit of the coset $M$ is $\{Ma:a\in A\}$, which is the whole coset space exactly when every $g\in G$ lies in some $Ma$, i.e., when $G=MA=AM$.
head: environment

label: lem:overgroup-restriction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:overgroup-restriction}
Let $A\leq E\leq G$. If $A$ is hereditarily $G$-permutable, then $A$ is hereditarily $E$-permutable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For $B\leq E$, by hereditary $G$-permutability of $A$ we have $x\in\langle A,B\rangle$ with $AB^x=B^xA$, and $\langle A,B\rangle\leq E$ since $A,B\leq E$. Consequently, the equality $AB^x=B^xA$ establishes hereditary $E$-permutability of $A$.
head: environment

label: lem:quotient-inheritance
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:quotient-inheritance}
Let $A\leq E$ and $N\unlhd E$. If $A$ is hereditarily $E$-permutable, then $AN/N$ is hereditarily $(E/N)$-permutable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\rho:E\to E/N$ be the quotient map. For a subgroup $T\leq E/N$, choose $B=\rho^{-1}(T)$. Then $BN/N\leq E/N$ and $T=BN/N$. By hereditary $E$-permutability of $A$ for $B$, we have $x\in\langle A,B\rangle$ with $AB^x=B^xA$. Taking the images of both sides of this equality in the quotient of $E$ by $N$, namely $E/N$, gives
$$
        (AN/N)(BN/N)^{xN}=(BN/N)^{xN}(AN/N),
$$
and $xN\in\langle AN/N,BN/N\rangle$.
head: environment

label: lem:almost-simple-core-free
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:almost-simple-core-free}
Let $S\leq E\leq \operatorname{Aut}(S)$ with $S$ nonabelian simple. A subgroup $H\leq E$ is core-free in $E$ if and only if $S\nleq H$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If $S\leq H$, then $S\leq\operatorname{Core}_E(H)$, so $H$ is not core-free in $E$. Conversely, suppose that $N=\operatorname{Core}_E(H)\neq1$. Since $N\unlhd E$, the subgroup $N\cap S$ is normal in $S$. If $N\cap S=1$, then $[N,S]\leq N\cap S=1$, so $N$ centralizes $S$. Together with $N\leq\operatorname{Aut}(S)$, this centralization implies that $N=1$, a contradiction. Hence $N\cap S=S$, and $S\leq N\leq H$.
head: environment

label: lem:normal-intersection-transfer
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:normal-intersection-transfer}
Let $A\leq G$ be hereditarily $G$-permutable, let $N\unlhd G$, and let $K=A\cap N$. Then $K$ is ordinarily $N$-permutable in $N$. For every $H\leq N$ there is $n\in N$ with
$$
        KH^n=H^nK.
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Fix $H\leq N$ and let $R=\langle A,H\rangle$. By hereditary $G$-permutability of $A$, we choose $x\in R$ with $AH^x=H^xA$. Since $N\unlhd G$, we have $R\leq AN=NA$, so we may write $x=nl$ with $n\in N$, $l\in A$. We take the intersection of both sides of $AH^x=H^xA$ with $N$. As $H^x\leq N$, this intersection gives
$$
        (A\cap N)H^x=H^x(A\cap N).
$$
Now $H^x=(H^n)^l$ and $A\cap N\unlhd A$. Conjugating the equality $(A\cap N)H^x=H^x(A\cap N)$ by $l^{-1}$, we obtain that $KH^n=H^nK$ with $n\in N$. Thus, the equality establishes ordinary $N$-permutability of $K$ only, and says nothing about hereditary permutability of the various subgroups of $A$.
head: environment

label: rem:actual-levi
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:actual-levi}
At each parabolic descent step, we study the image of $A$ in the full Levi quotient specified at that step. In particular, we include the diagonal part of this quotient as well as its simple socle. In the linear case the quotient is a group $E$ with
$$
        \operatorname{PSL}_m(q)\leq E\leq \operatorname{PGL}_m(q),
$$
and by Lemma \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance} the image of $A$ is hereditarily $E$-permutable. Consequently, we state the lemmas describing the descent and its alternatives for $E$ rather than for the socle of $E$, $\operatorname{PSL}_m(q)$. The parabolic and Levi structure used in these steps is standard. For this parabolic and Levi structure, we follow Carter \cite{Carter1985}, Malle and Testerman \cite{MalleTesterman2011}, and Kleidman and Liebeck \cite{KleidmanLiebeck1990}.
head: environment

label: thm:split-linear
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:split-linear}
For every nonabelian simple group $G=\operatorname{PSL}_n(q)$ there is no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

label: prop:sl-parabolic-containment
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:sl-parabolic-containment}
$A$ is contained in a proper parabolic subgroup of $G$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $A$ is not contained in a proper parabolic subgroup of $G$. Let $B$ be a Borel subgroup of $G$. By hereditary permutability of $A$ in $G$ there is $x\in G$ with $AB^x=B^xA$, so $AB^x$ is a subgroup. If $AB^x<G$, then a maximal subgroup containing $AB^x$ would contain the Borel subgroup $B^x$ and hence be parabolic. This would contradict the assumption that $A$ lies in no proper parabolic subgroup of $G$. Therefore, $G=AB^x$. Because $A<G$, we choose a maximal subgroup $M$ with $A\leq M<G$. Since $A\leq M$, we have a factorization
$$
        G=MB^x
$$
with solvable factor $B^x$.

We now use the classification of factorizations with a solvable factor, due to Li and Xia \cite[Theorem 1.1 and Tables 1.1--1.2]{LiXia2022}. The relevant linear rows are Table 1.1, rows 1--2, and Table 1.2, rows 6--9, which are all the rows of \cite[Tables 1.1--1.2]{LiXia2022} with linear socle $\operatorname{PSL}_n(q)$, $n\geq3$. Let $p$ be the characteristic of the field. In each of these listed linear rows the solvable factor has a smaller $p$-part than a Borel subgroup of $\operatorname{PSL}_n(q)$. The $p$-part for a Borel subgroup is
$$
        |B|_p=q^{n(n-1)/2},
$$
since type $A_{n-1}$ has $n(n-1)/2$ positive roots \cite{Carter1985}. The following table compares the two $p$-parts.
$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{socle} & \text{solvable-factor row} & \text{solvable }p\text{-part} & \text{Borel }p\text{-part}\\\hline
\operatorname{PSL}_n(q) & \widehat{\operatorname{GL}}_1(q^n):n & |n|_p & q^{n(n-1)/2}\\
\operatorname{PSL}_4(q) & q^3:((q^3-1)/(4,q-1))\cdot 3 & q^3 |3|_p & q^6\\
\operatorname{PSL}_4(3) & 2^4:5:4 & 1 & 3^6\\
\operatorname{PSL}_4(3) & 3^3:13:3 & 3^4 & 3^6\\
\operatorname{PSL}_4(4) & 2^6:63:3 & 2^6 & 2^{12}\\
\operatorname{PSL}_5(2) & 31:5 & 1 & 2^{10}
\end{array}
$$
We have $|n|_p<q^{n(n-1)/2}$ for $n\geq3$, and $q^3|3|_p<q^6$ in the second row (including $p=3$). Thus, $B^x$ cannot be one of the solvable factors in the listed linear rows, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:sl-line-hyperplane
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sl-line-hyperplane}
Suppose that $A\leq P_j$, where $P_j$ is the stabilizer in $G$ of a $j$-dimensional subspace $U$ of $V$ with $1\leq j\leq n-1$. Then, after relabelling, $A$ stabilizes a line $\ell$ and a hyperplane $H$ of $V$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We use Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} for the point stabilizer $P_1$ in $G$, which is maximal in $G$. If $G=AP_1^x$, then $A$ is transitive on the projective points of $V$. However, $A$ stabilizes $U$ and so maps the nonempty proper set of projective points in $U$ to itself. This contradicts the transitivity of $A$. Hence $A\leq P_1^x$ for some $x$, i.e., $A$ stabilizes a line of $V$. Similarly, hereditary permutability of $A$ with the hyperplane stabilizer in $G$, together with the nontransitivity of $A$ on hyperplanes, shows that $A\leq P_{n-1}^y$ for some $y$.
head: environment

label: lem:sl-actual-quotient-trichotomy
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sl-actual-quotient-trichotomy}
Let $m\geq3$ and let $S=\operatorname{PSL}_m(q)$. Suppose that $S\leq E\leq\operatorname{PGL}_m(q)$. Let $C\leq E$ be hereditarily $E$-permutable. Then we have three alternatives for $C$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item $C\geq S$.
\item $C$ lies in the normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic subgroup of $S$. Let $Q$ denote this proper parabolic subgroup. We take the inverse image of this proper parabolic subgroup of $S$ under $\pi:P_0\to E$. Let $U_1<\cdots<U_a$ be the flag in $U_0=F_j/F_{j-1}$ stabilized by $Q$. For the quotient map $\tau_j:F_j\to U_0$, write $Y_i=\tau_j^{-1}(U_i)$. The new flag inserts the chain $F_{j-1}<Y_1<\cdots<Y_a<F_j$ between the same two terms $F_{j-1}$ and $F_j$ of $\mathcal F_0$. All other terms of $\mathcal F_0$ remain in the new flag.
\item After every possible extension of the flag through the parabolic subgroups in (2), let $\mathcal F$ be the extended flag in $U_0$, the natural module for $E$. Let $P_{\mathcal F}=\operatorname{Stab}_E(\mathcal F)$. The Levi quotient is $P_{\mathcal F}/R_u(P_{\mathcal F})$, which we denote by $L_{\mathcal F}$. After adding the zero subspace $0$ and the whole space $U_0$, write $\mathcal F$ as $0=W_0<W_1<\cdots<W_b=U_0$. The linear factors of $L_{\mathcal F}$ correspond to the actions on $W_i/W_{i-1}$. Under these actions, the image of $C$ in each simple factor of the semisimple part of $L_{\mathcal F}$ is trivial. Consequently, we continue with the Borel argument for the extended flag.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $C\not\geq S$ and $C$ does not lie in the normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic subgroup of $S$. Suppose also that the semisimple image of $C$ in the projective Levi quotient $E$ with simple socle $S$ is nontrivial. We must derive a contradiction from these assumptions. We let $B_S$ be a Borel subgroup of $S$ and $B_E=N_E(B_S)$. Since a diagonal projective element can be represented by a diagonal matrix and so normalizes the standard Borel subgroup of $S$, $B_E$ maps onto $E/S$ under the quotient map from $E$ to $E/S$. By hereditary $E$-permutability of $C$ for $B_E$, we have a conjugate $B_E^x$ with
$$
        H=CB_E^x
$$
a subgroup of $E$. If $H<E$, then take a maximal subgroup $M<E$ containing $H$. Since $B_E^x$ maps onto $E/S$, $M$ cannot contain $S$: otherwise $M/S=E/S$ and $M=E$. Hence $M\cap S$ is a proper subgroup of $S$ containing the Borel subgroup $B_S^x$. Therefore, it is parabolic. Consequently, $C\leq M\leq N_E(M\cap S)$, so $C$ lies in the normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic subgroup of $S$, contrary to assumption. Therefore,
$$
        E=CB_E^x,
$$
a factorization of the almost simple group $E$ with solvable factor $B_E^x$. Neither $C$ nor $B_E ^x$ contains $S$, so both are core-free in $E$ (Lemma \ref{lem:almost-simple-core-free}), and $B_E^x\cap S$ has the same $p$-part of its order as a Borel subgroup of $S$. As shown in Proposition \ref{prop:sl-parabolic-containment}, none of the linear rows of Li and Xia has a solvable factor whose order has a $p$-part at least as large as that of a Borel subgroup of $S$ when $m\geq3$. This contradiction completes the proof.
head: environment

label: lem:sl-root-line-module-obstruction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sl-root-line-module-obstruction}
Let $V$ be a vector space over $K=\mathbb{F}_q$, written additively, and suppose that
$$
        F=VA
$$
is a semidirect product with $A\cap V=1$ and $A$ acting $K$-linearly on $V$. We write $\bar A$ for the image of the action of $A$ on $V$ in $\operatorname{GL}_K(V)$. If $A$ is hereditarily $F$-permutable and $U\leq V$ is a $K$-line, then $\bar A$ stabilizes some $K$-line of $V$. In particular, if $\bar A$ has no invariant $K$-line on $V$, then no subgroup $A$ satisfying these hypotheses exists.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By hereditary $F$-permutability of $A$ with $U$, we have $x\in F$ with $AU^x=U^xA$ a subgroup of $F$. Since $V\unlhd F$ and the action of $A$ on $V$ is $K$-linear, $U^x$ is again a $K$-line. The equality $A\cap V=1$ also gives
$$
        (AU^x)\cap V=U^x
$$
Hence, for every $a\in A$,
$$
        aU^xa^{-1}\leq (AU^x)\cap V=U^x,
$$
so $A$ stabilizes the $K$-line $U^x$. Therefore, $\bar A$ stabilizes the line $U^x$ as well. The existence of this invariant line is impossible if $\bar A$ has no invariant $K$-line.
head: environment

label: lem:sl-nonincident-full-cover
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sl-nonincident-full-cover}
Suppose that $A \leq G = {\rm PSL}_n (q)={\rm PSL} (V)$ stabilizes the pair $\ell, H$ (i.e. $\ell$ is a line and $H$ is a hyperplane in $V$) with $V=\ell\oplus H$. If $\dim H\geq3$ and the image $\bar{A}$ of $A$ on $H$ contains $\operatorname{PSL}(H)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_{\dim H}(q)$, then these conditions are incompatible. If $\dim H=2$ and the image $\bar{A}$ of $A$ on $H$ stabilizes no line, then these conditions are also incompatible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $\dim H\geq3$, and test hereditary permutability of $A$ in $G$ against a $2$-space stabilizer $P_2$ in $G$, which is maximal in $G$. Since $A$ fixes $\ell$, the group $A$ maps the nonempty proper set of $2$-spaces containing $\ell$ to itself. Using Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} we get either $G = A P_2 ^x$ or $A \leq P_2 ^x$. If $G = A P_2 ^x$, then $A$ acts transitively on the 2-dimensional subspaces of $V$, a contradiction. Hence $G = A P_2 ^x$ cannot occur and $A$ stabilizes some $2$-space $X$. Under the quotient map $V\to V/\ell$, the image of $X$ is $(X+\ell)/\ell$. This subspace of $V/\ell\cong H$ has dimension $1$ or $2$, so the image $ \bar{A} \geq \operatorname{PSL}(H)$ of $A$ would stabilize a proper nonzero subspace of $H$, a contradiction.

Now let $\dim H=2$, so $G=\operatorname{PSL}_3(q)$. If the image $C$ of $A$ on $H$ fixes a line $K\leq H$, then we extend the flag $(\ell)$ to $(\ell<\ell\oplus K)$ and continue the descent. Its full chain is $0<\ell<\ell\oplus K<V$. Otherwise let $C$ be the image of $A$ on $H$, with no invariant line. Consider the block diagonal stabilizer of the decomposition $\ell\oplus H$ in $G$. The symbol $\operatorname{Hom}(\ell,H)$ denotes the additive group of $\mathbb{F}_q$-linear maps from $\ell$ to $H$. We work in the subgroup generated by this stabilizer and the unipotent radical of $\operatorname{Stab}_G(H)$, written as
$$
        V_+=\operatorname{Hom}(\ell,H).
$$ The parabolics $\operatorname{Stab}_G(H)$ and $\operatorname{Stab}_G(\ell)$ are opposite. Their common Levi subgroup is the block diagonal stabilizer of $\ell\oplus H$ in $G$. The subgroup generated by this Levi subgroup and $V_+$ is a semidirect product. Every nonidentity element of $V_+$ (viewed as a subgroup of $G$) moves the line $\ell$, sending a spanning vector $v$ to $v+\varphi(v)$ with $\varphi(v)\in H$. Since $A$ stabilizes $\ell$, we have $A\cap V_+=1$. The induced $C$-module $V_+$ is the natural module of dimension two for $C$. Using Lemma \ref{lem:sl-root-line-module-obstruction} for a line over $\mathbb{F}_q$ in $V_+$ forces $C$ to fix a line of $H$, contrary to assumption.
head: environment

label: lem:sl-incident-full-cover-large
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sl-incident-full-cover-large}
Suppose that $A \leq G$ stabilizes the flag $\ell<H$ in $V$ and the image of $A$ on $W=H/\ell$ contains $\operatorname{PSL}_d(q)$ with $d=n-2\geq3$. These conditions on the flag and the image of $A$ are incompatible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We let $Y\leq V$ be an $A$-stable subspace. Because $A$ stabilizes $\ell<H$, the dimensions
$$
        \dim(Y\cap\ell),~
        \dim\bigl(((Y\cap H)+\ell)/\ell\bigr),~
        \dim\bigl((Y+H)/H\bigr)
$$
are invariant under the action of $A$ on the three factors $\ell$, $W=H/\ell$, and $V/H$. The image of $A$ on $W$ contains $\operatorname{PSL}_d(q)$. Under the hypotheses of the lemma, the natural module of $\operatorname{PSL}_d(q)$ is irreducible. Hence the subquotient $((Y\cap H)+\ell)/\ell$ is $0$ or all of $W$. The subspaces $Y\cap\ell$ and $(Y+H)/H$, corresponding to the first and third dimensions, are of dimension at most one. Hence every $A$-stable subspace of $V$ has dimension in
$$
        \{0,1,2,d,d+1,d+2\}.
$$

For a $k$-subspace stabilizer $P_k$ in $G$, Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} gives either an $A$-stable $k$-subspace or $G=AP_k^x$. By Lemma \ref{lem:factorization-coset-transitivity}, the equality $G=AP_k^x$ would make $A$ transitive on $k$-subspaces $X$ of $V$. Since $A$ does not change the pair $(\dim(X\cap\ell),\dim(X\cap H))$, transitivity is impossible for $2\leq k\leq n-1$. So $A$ stabilizes a $k$-subspace for every $k$ in the range $2\leq k\leq n-1$.

If $d\geq4$, then take $k=3$. Then $3\notin\{0,1,2,d,d+1,d+2\}$, a contradiction. If $d=3$, then by testing hereditary permutability of $A$ with $P_2$, we have an $A$-stable $2$-subspace $X$ (by the conclusion for $k =2$ obtained from Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product}). If $X\leq H$, then $X$ or $(X+\ell)/\ell$ is a proper nonzero $A$-invariant subspace of $W$, impossible. If $X\not\leq H$ and $\ell\not\leq X$, then $((X\cap H)+\ell)/\ell$ is an $A$-invariant line of $W$, again impossible. The only remaining position of $X$ relative to $\ell$ and $H$ is
$$
        \ell<X\not\leq H.
$$
Under the quotient map from $V$ to $V/\ell$, the image $X/\ell$ is a line not contained in the hyperplane $H/\ell$, while the image of $A$ on $H/\ell$ contains $\operatorname{PSL}_3(q)$. Therefore, the line $X/\ell$ and the hyperplane $H/\ell$ in $V/\ell$ give the configuration described in Lemma \ref{lem:sl-nonincident-full-cover}, a contradiction.
head: environment

label: lem:sl-incident-full-cover-d2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sl-incident-full-cover-d2}
Let $G=\operatorname{PSL}_4(q) = \operatorname{PSL} (V)$, and suppose that $A$ stabilizes a flag
$$
        \ell<H,~ \dim\ell=1,~ \dim H=3,
$$
with the image $\bar{A}$ of $A$ on $W=H/\ell$ stabilizing no line of $W$. These conditions on the flag and the image of $A$ are incompatible.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Choose a complement to $\ell$ in $H$. The map $H\to H/\ell$ identifies this complement with $W=H/\ell$, and we denote the complement by the same symbol $W$. We choose a line $m$ complementary to $H$ in $V$. We fix a decomposition
$$
        V=\ell\oplus W\oplus m,~ H=\ell\oplus W.
$$
Let $P=\operatorname{Stab}_G(\ell<H)$ be the parabolic subgroup of $G$ stabilizing the flag $\ell<H$. Inside $P$, the unipotent subgroups used in this proof are
$$
        U_-=\operatorname{Hom}(W,\ell),~ U_0=\operatorname{Hom}(m,\ell),~ U_+=\operatorname{Hom}(m,W),
$$
and the image of $A$ on $W$ acts on $U_-$ as the dual natural module and on $U_+$ as the natural module.

Testing hereditary permutability of $A$ in $G$ against a $2$-subspace stabilizer $P_2$ in $G$ forces $A$ to fix some $2$-subspace $X$, i.e., $A \leq P_2 ^x$ for some $x \in G$. Otherwise $G = A P_2 ^x$ and $A$ would be transitive on $2$-subspaces of $V$. This is impossible since $A$ fixes the flag $\ell<H$. By hypothesis, the image $\bar{A}$ of $A$ on $W$ has no invariant line. Each of the positions $\ell<X\leq H$ and ($X\cap H$ a line with $\ell\not\leq X$) would produce an $A$-invariant line of $W=H/\ell$. Hence neither position is possible. There are two possible positions of $X$ relative to the flag $\ell<H$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item $X\leq H$ and $\ell\not\leq X$. Then $H=\ell\oplus X$, and fixing $X$ makes the $U_-=\operatorname{Hom}(X,\ell)$ component of $A$ trivial. The quotient $P/(U_0U_+)$ of the flag stabilizer in $G$ by $U_0U_+$ is a semidirect product $U_-\rtimes C$. The image $C$ of $A$ on $U_-$ must be trivial. Also, $C$ has no invariant line on the dual natural module $U_-$.
\item $\ell\leq X$ and $X\not\leq H$. Then $X=\ell\oplus m'$ with a line $m'$ mapping nontrivially to $V/H$. Since $A$ fixes $X$, the $U_+=\operatorname{Hom}(m,W)$ component of $A$ is trivial. The quotient $P/(U_0U_-)$ of the flag stabilizer in $G$ by $U_0U_-$ is the semidirect product $U_+\rtimes C$. The image $C$ of $A$ on $U_+$ meets $U_+$ trivially. Also, $C$ has no invariant line on the natural module $U_+$.
\end{enumerate}
The module of dimension two is $U_-$ for position (1) of $X$ and $U_+$ for position (2). We choose a line over $\mathbb{F}_q$ in the module corresponding to the position of $X$. Lemma \ref{lem:sl-root-line-module-obstruction} then forces $C$ to fix a line of the natural or dual natural module, contradicting the hypothesis that the image of $A$ on $W$ has no invariant line.

title: Remark
body_md: Lemma \ref{lem:sl-incident-full-cover-d2} proves the incompatibility for $d=2$, where the $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ theorem alone is insufficient. The theorem \cite[Proposition 1]{GT2023} forbids proper hereditarily permutable subgroups of $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$. However, the image of $A$ on $W$ may equal the whole group $E$ induced by the projective action of $\operatorname{Stab}_G(\ell<H)$ on $W$, so that image need not be proper. Lemma \ref{lem:sl-root-line-module-obstruction}, used with a line in the corresponding natural or dual natural module, forces this image of $A$ to fix a line of $W$, contrary to the hypothesis in the dimension two case.

label: lem:pgl2-borel
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:pgl2-borel}
Let
$$
       S= \operatorname{PSL}_2(q)\leq E\leq\operatorname{PGL}_2(q),~ C\leq B_E,
$$
where $B_E$ is a point stabilizer in $E$ on the projective line, and suppose that $E\not\cong\operatorname{PGL}_2(2)$. If $C$ is hereditarily $E$-permutable, then $C=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof into three steps.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 1.}] $C=1$ if $q=3$ or $C\leq S$.
\end{itemize}
We let $S=\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$. We begin with the case $q=3$, where $S\cong A_4$ is not simple, so the $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ theorem does not cover this group and we argue directly. We have $E\in\{A_4,S_4\}$ and $C$ lies in a point stabilizer $B_E$ of $E$ on the projective line. If $E\cong A_4$, then $B_E\cong C_3$. For the only nontrivial candidate $C=B_E$, permuting with the subgroup generated by an involution of $A_4$ would produce a subgroup of order $6$, and $A_4$ has none. Therefore, the candidate $C=B_E$ is not hereditarily $E$-permutable. If $E\cong S_4=\operatorname{PGL}_2(3)$, then $B_E\cong S_3$, and we test each nontrivial subgroup of $S_3$ for hereditary $S_4$-permutability. By Lemma \ref{lem:generated-hereditary-formulation} the conjugating element may be taken in $\langle C,H\rangle$, and for each candidate $C$ we choose a subgroup $H$ such that no conjugate of $H$ in $\langle C,H\rangle$ permutes with $C$. For a candidate $C$ of order $3$ and a subgroup $H$ generated by an involution without fixed points, $\langle C,H\rangle=A_4$. This group has no subgroup of order $6$, so the order-$6$ product $CH^x$ is not a subgroup for any $x \in \langle C,H \rangle$. The subgroup generated by an involution fixing a point would instead lie in the same point stabilizer $S_3$ as $C$ and permute with $C$. For a candidate $C$ generated by a transposition, choose a subgroup $H$ generated by a double transposition for which $\langle C,H\rangle$ is a Sylow $2$-subgroup $D_8$. Since no conjugate of $H$ in $\langle C,H\rangle$ permutes with $C$, the subgroup $C$ fails this permutability test with $H$. Finally consider $C=B_E$ and a subgroup $H$ generated by a double transposition. We have $\langle C,H\rangle=S_4$ and $B_E$ contains odd permutations, while every conjugate $H^x$ meets $B_E$ trivially, so $|B_EH^x|=12$ for all $x$. The unique subgroup of $S_4$ of order $12$ is $A_4$, which has no odd permutation, so $B_EH^x$ is not a subgroup for any $x$. Comparing $B_E$ with a second point stabilizer does not test failure of hereditary permutability, since the second point stabilizer is $S_4$-conjugate to $B_E$. These checks are confirmed by the computation of Appendix \ref{app:pgl2-small-certificate}, whose enumeration includes $q=3$. Hence $C=1$ when $q=3$, and we assume that $q\geq4$ from now on.

If $q$ is even, then $E=S$, and the conclusion $C=1$ follows from the $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ theorem \cite[Proposition 1]{GT2023}. More generally, we have $C=1$ whenever $E=S$. If $q$ is odd, then $q\geq5$ and $S=\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ is simple. If moreover $C\leq S$, then restricting the hereditary condition from $E$ to $S$ makes $C$ hereditarily $S$-permutable (Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction}), so $C=1$ by the $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ theorem (\cite[Proposition 1]{GT2023}).

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 2.}] If $q>11$, then $|C|\mid4$.
\end{itemize}
Therefore, we may assume that
$$
        q\geq5\text{ odd},~ E=\operatorname{PGL}_2(q),~ C\nleq S.
$$

Suppose that $q>11$. Let $D_-,D_+\leq S$ be the normalizers in $S$ of a split and of a nonsplit maximal torus of $S$, so
$$
        |D_-|=q-1,~ |D_+|=q+1.
$$
By Dickson's subgroup theorem \cite[\S260, Theorem 262]{Dickson1901}, $D_-$ and $D_+$ are maximal in $S$ for $q>11$. By hereditary $E$-permutability of $C$ with $D_-$, for some conjugate $D_-^x$, the product $H=CD_-^x$ is a subgroup. Since $C\leq B_E$, we have $|C|\leq|B_E|=q(q-1)$, so
$$
        |C|\,|D_-^x|\leq q(q-1)^2<q(q-1)(q+1)=|E|,
$$
and $H<E$. A maximal subgroup $M\geq H$ of $E$ does not contain $S$ (the subgroup $M$ contains an element outside $S$), so $M\cap S=D_-^x$ by maximality of $D_-^x$ in $S$. As $S\unlhd E$, $M\cap S\unlhd M$, whence
$$
        C\leq M\leq N_E(D_-^x),~ |C|\mid 2(q-1).
$$
Repeating the hereditary permutability test for $C$ with $D_+$ and using the order bound for $C$ from $|C|\mid 2(q-1)$, we obtain
$$
        |C|\,|D_+^y|\leq 2(q-1)(q+1)<|E|,
$$
so $CD_+^y<E$ and $C\leq N_E(D_+^y)$, and hence $|C|\mid 2(q+1)$. Therefore,
$$
        |C|\mid\bigl(2(q-1),2(q+1)\bigr)=4.
$$

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 3.}] $C=1$ in all cases.
\end{itemize}
Since $C\leq B_E\cong q:(q-1)$ and $|C|$ is prime to the characteristic $q$, $C$ fixes a point of the affine line and so is conjugate inside $B_E$ into the split torus of $E$ contained in $B_E$. As $C\nleq S$, the only possibilities for $C$ are a subgroup generated by an involution outside $S$ or a cyclic group of order $4$ not contained in $S$.

Suppose that $|C|=2$. After conjugating $C$ in $E$ we may take $C=\langle c\rangle$ with $c\colon z\mapsto-z$. With
$$
        h\colon z\mapsto\frac{z+1}{z-1},~ H_0=\langle h\rangle,~ F=\langle c,h\rangle,
$$
we have $F\cong D_8$, with the generators $c$ and $h$ in the two different conjugacy classes of reflections. No $F$-conjugate of $H_0$ equals or commutes with $C$. Two subgroups of order $2$ permute if and only if their nonidentity elements commute, so $C$ is not hereditarily $F$-permutable, a contradiction.

Suppose that $|C|=4$. Since $q$ is odd, the unipotent radical of $B_E$ has odd order, so $C$ embeds in the cyclic split torus of $E$ in $B_E$ of order $q-1$. Therefore, $4\mid q-1$. Let $r\colon z\mapsto iz$ with $i$ of order $4$ and $i^2=-1$. Then $C=\langle r\rangle$ is the unique order-$4$ subgroup of this torus. As $C\nleq S$, the generator $i$ is a nonsquare in $\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ (a square generator would mean that $C\leq S$). We consider this cyclic subgroup of order four only when an element $i$ of order four that is a nonsquare in $\mathbb{F}_q^\times$ exists. With the element $h$ acting by $z\mapsto\frac{z+1}{z-1}$, the group $F=\langle r,h\rangle$ is the subgroup $S_4$ of $\operatorname{PGL}_2(q)$. Let $H_0\leq F$ have order $3$. If $CH_0^x=H_0^xC$ for some $x\in F$, then $CH_0^x$ is a subgroup of $S_4$ of order $12$ containing an element of order $4$. However, the only subgroup of $S_4$ of order $12$ is $A_4$, which has no element of order $4$. This contradiction settles $|C|=4$.

Finally, for the field sizes $q\in\{5,7,9,11\}$ we verify $C=1$ by a direct computation in $\operatorname{PGL}_2(q)$. We enumerate the subgroups of a point stabilizer in $E$. For each nontrivial candidate $C$, the computation finds an element $h\in E$ and tests $C$ against the cyclic subgroup $\langle h\rangle$ inside $\langle C,h\rangle$. No $x\in\langle C,h\rangle$ satisfies $C\langle h\rangle^x=\langle h\rangle^xC$. Consequently, every nontrivial candidate $C$ fails to be hereditarily $E$-permutable in $E$. The subgroup $\langle C,h\rangle$ is generated by $C$ and this chosen element $h$ (Appendix \ref{app:pgl2-small-certificate}). Hence $C=1$ for every field size $q$ covered by the lemma.

label: lem:sl-borel
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:sl-borel}
Let
$$
        \operatorname{PSL}_m(q)\leq E\leq\operatorname{PGL}_m(q),~ m\geq2,
$$
and let $B_E$ be the normalizer in $E$ of the upper triangular Borel subgroup of the socle of $E$. Apart from $(m,q,E)=(2,2,\operatorname{PGL}_2(2))$, if $C\leq B_E$ is hereditarily $E$-permutable, then $C=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We induct on $m$. For $m=2$, the conclusion follows from Lemma \ref{lem:pgl2-borel}, apart from the $\operatorname{PGL}_2(2)$ case. The case $m=3$, $q=2$ is handled by the isomorphism $\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)$ \cite[p. 3]{Wilson2009} together with the $\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)$ theorem \cite[Proposition 1]{GT2023}, which avoids the (false) $\operatorname{PGL}_2(2)$ case.

Assume that $m\geq3$ and $(m,q)\neq(3,2)$. The parabolic subgroups $P_1$ and $P_{m-1}$ of $E$ stabilize a line and a hyperplane, respectively. Choose an $\mathbb{F}_q$-basis $(e_1,\ldots,e_m)$ of the natural space $\mathbb{F}_q^m$ in which $B_E$ is upper triangular. Write $Q_1=\mathbb{F}_q^m/\langle e_1\rangle$ and $Q_{m-1}=\langle e_1,\ldots,e_{m-1}\rangle$. The lower right block acts on $Q_1$, and the upper left block acts on $Q_{m-1}$. Let $\rho_i:P_i\to\operatorname{PGL}(Q_i)$ be these projective actions, and let $E_i=\rho_i(P_i)$ for $i\in\{1,m-1\}$. We take the images of $C$ under the projective actions of these subgroups on the lower right and upper left blocks, respectively. For each of $P_1$ and $P_{m-1}$, we quotient the parabolic subgroup by the elements acting as scalars on the corresponding block. These projective factors of the Levi quotients are projective linear of dimension $m-1$ \cite[Proposition 26.1(b)]{MalleTesterman2011}. By Lemma \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance}, the images $\rho_i(C)$ of $C$ in these quotients are hereditarily $E_i$-permutable for $i\in\{1,m-1\}$. By induction, both images of $C$ in the projective actions on the lower right and upper left $(m-1)\times(m-1)$ blocks are trivial. Hence the diagonal part of $C$ and its components in all root subgroups except the subgroup corresponding to the highest root are trivial. In upper triangular terms,
$$
        C\leq U_{1m}.
$$
If $q\geq4$, then the opposite root subgroups $U_{1m}$ and $U_{m1}$ generate a subgroup $R\cong\operatorname{SL}_2(q)$ \cite{Carter1985}. A nontrivial scalar in the centre of $\operatorname{SL}_m(q)$ acts nontrivially on the middle coordinates $2,\dots,m-1$ (nonempty as $m\geq3$). By contrast, the group $R$ fixes these middle coordinates, so the embedding of $R$ in $E$ is faithful. Since $C\leq U_{1m}$ is unipotent, $C\cap Z(R)=1$. By Lemmas \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} and \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance}, the image $\bar C$ of $C$ in $R/Z(R)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ is hereditarily $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$-permutable and isomorphic to $C$. The $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ theorem \cite[Proposition 1]{GT2023} (valid as $q\geq4$) shows that $\bar C=1$, hence $C=1$. There remain $q\in\{2,3\}$, where $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ is not simple. If $q=2$, then $m\geq4$. Pick $j$ with $1<j<m$. The root subgroups on coordinates $1,j,m$ generate a subgroup with simple quotient $\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)$ \cite[p. 3]{Wilson2009}. Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} and the $\operatorname{PSL}_2(7)$ theorem \cite[Proposition 1]{GT2023} then show that $C=1$. If $q=3$, then $\bar C$ is the image of $C$ obtained by projecting through the parabolic subgroups $P_1$ and $P_{m-1}$ of $E$. In this case, $\bar C$ is a hereditarily $(R/Z(R))$-permutable subgroup of $R/Z(R)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(3)\cong A_4$. This image has order dividing $3$. Were $\bar C\neq1$, the subgroup $\bar C$ would permute with the subgroup generated by an involution of $A_4$ to produce a subgroup of order $6$, which $A_4$ lacks. Hence $\bar C=1$ and $C=1$.

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A<G=\operatorname{PSL}_n(q)$ be proper, nontrivial, and hereditarily $G$-permutable. For $n=2$, we use the known theorem for linear groups of dimension two \cite[Proposition 1]{GT2023}, so we assume that $n\geq3$. By Proposition \ref{prop:sl-parabolic-containment}, $A$ lies in a proper parabolic subgroup of $G$. Lemma \ref{lem:sl-line-hyperplane} gives, after relabelling, a line $\ell$ and a hyperplane $H$ in $V$ stabilized by $A$.

Suppose that $\ell\not\leq H$, so $V=\ell\oplus H$ and the image $C$ of $A$ on $H$ is hereditarily $E$-permutable in a group $\operatorname{PSL}_{n-1}(q)\leq E\leq\operatorname{PGL}_{n-1}(q)$. For a flag $\mathcal F_H=(H_1<\cdots<H_t)$ in $H$ fixed by $C$, the corresponding flag in $V$ extends $(\ell)$ and has full chain $0<\ell<\ell\oplus H_1<\cdots<\ell\oplus H_t<V$. For each additional term $K$ of the flag in $H$, the corresponding additional term in $V$ is $\ell\oplus K$. If $n-1\geq3$, then we use Lemma \ref{lem:sl-actual-quotient-trichotomy}. The case in which $C$ contains the socle of $E$ cannot occur by Lemma \ref{lem:sl-nonincident-full-cover}. When $C$ lies in the normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic subgroup of the socle of $E$, we extend the flag. Suppose that $C$ lies in no such normalizer in $E$ and does not contain the socle. Testing $C$ through the normalizer in $E$ of a Borel subgroup of the socle of $E$ gives a contradiction in this case. This follows the argument in Proposition \ref{prop:sl-parabolic-containment}. Let $\mathcal F_H$ be the extended flag in $H$, and let $P_H=\operatorname{Stab}_E(\mathcal F_H)$. Its Levi quotient is $L_H=P_H/R_u(P_H)$. When the image of $C$ in each simple factor of the semisimple part of $L_H$ is trivial, we use Lemma \ref{lem:sl-borel}. If $n-1=2$, then we extend the flag when $C$ lies in the normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic subgroup of the socle of $E$. An image $C$ with no invariant line is impossible by the argument in dimension two of Lemma \ref{lem:sl-nonincident-full-cover}. When the image of $C$ in every simple factor of this Levi quotient is trivial, we again use Lemma \ref{lem:sl-borel}.

Next suppose that $\ell\leq H$, and let $W=H/\ell$. For the quotient map $\tau:H\to W$, a flag $W_1<\cdots<W_t$ in $W$ fixed by the image of $A$ gives the extended flag $\ell<\tau^{-1}(W_1)<\cdots<\tau^{-1}(W_t)<H$ in $V$. This extends the original flag $(\ell<H)$ by inserting the inverse images of the new quotient subspaces. If $n=3$, then $A$ stabilizes the complete flag $0<\ell<H<V$, whose nonzero terms have dimensions $1,2,3$. Consequently, it lies in a Borel subgroup of $G$ and must be trivial by Lemma \ref{lem:sl-borel}. So assume that $n-2\geq2$. The image $C$ of $A$ on $W$ is hereditarily $E$-permutable in a group $\operatorname{PSL}_{n-2}(q)\leq E\leq\operatorname{PGL}_{n-2}(q)$. If $n-2\geq3$, then we use Lemma \ref{lem:sl-actual-quotient-trichotomy}. The possibility that $C$ contains the socle of $E$ contradicts Lemma \ref{lem:sl-incident-full-cover-large}. When $C$ lies in the normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic subgroup of the socle of $E$, we extend the flag. Suppose that $C$ lies in no such normalizer and does not contain the socle. We test $C$ through the normalizer in $E$ of a Borel subgroup of the socle of $E$. Let $\mathcal F_W$ be the extended flag in $W$, and let $P_W=\operatorname{Stab}_E(\mathcal F_W)$. Its Levi quotient is $L_W=P_W/R_u(P_W)$. When the image of $C$ in every simple factor of the semisimple part of $L_W$ is trivial, we use Lemma \ref{lem:sl-borel}. If $n-2=2$, then we proceed as follows. When $C$ lies in the normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic subgroup of the socle of $E$, we extend the flag. Every image of $A$ lying in no such normalizer and having no invariant line contradicts Lemma \ref{lem:sl-incident-full-cover-d2}. If the image of $C$ in every simple factor of this Levi quotient is trivial, then $A$ must again be trivial by Lemma \ref{lem:sl-borel}.

At each step at which the descent continues, the dimension of the space on which the linear Levi quotient at that step acts strictly decreases. Therefore, the descent reaches either the $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ base \cite[Proposition 1]{GT2023} or Lemma \ref{lem:sl-borel}. In either case, these results forbid a proper nontrivial subgroup with the hereditary permutability property in the image of the projective action at that step of the descent. This contradiction proves the theorem.

title: Theorem

For the simple group $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ there is no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.

label: thm:unitary-low-bases
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unitary-low-bases}
We use three results of low rank.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item For $Q\geq4$, $\operatorname{PSL}_2(Q)$ has no proper nontrivial hereditarily $\operatorname{PSL}_2(Q)$-permutable subgroup.
\item For $Q\geq4$, a proper ordinary $\operatorname{PSL}_2(Q)$-permutable subgroup of $\operatorname{PSL}_2(Q)$, if such an ordinary permutable subgroup exists, has order $2$.
\item For $Q\geq3$, $\operatorname{PSU}_3(Q)$ has no proper nontrivial hereditarily $\operatorname{PSU}_3(Q)$-permutable subgroup.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The nonexistence of proper nontrivial hereditarily $\operatorname{PSL}_2(Q)$-permutable subgroups is proved in \cite[Proposition 1]{GT2023}. For $Q>4$, the conclusion about subgroups of order two for ordinary $\operatorname{PSL}_2(Q)$-permutable subgroups is \cite[Theorem 1]{GT2025}. For $Q=4$, we use $\operatorname{PSL}_2(4)\cong A_5$, for which the examples of subgroups of order two are described in \cite[Example 1]{GT2022}. The nonexistence of proper nontrivial hereditarily permutable subgroups of $\operatorname{PSU}_3(Q)$ for $Q\geq3$ is proved in \cite[Theorem 2]{GT2025}. (The inheritance of hereditary permutability by quotient images is \cite[Lemma 5]{GT2025}. Lemma \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance} provides the short proof we use.)

title: Remark
body_md: We consider the permutation image of $A$ on the lines of a self-polar simplex. In this argument, we use the \emph{ordinary} theorem of Yang and Galt on $A_p$-permutable subgroups of alternating groups of prime degree. The theorem of Yang and Galt applies to the intersection of the permutation image of $A$ with the alternating group of prime degree. Indeed, Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-alt-transfer} establishes ordinary $A_p$-permutability of this intersection. The theorem on hereditary permutability in alternating groups is used in the proof of the main theorem, after the four classical families have been treated.

label: lem:unitary-weyl-normalization
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-weyl-normalization}
Let $E=\bar D\rtimes S_m$ be the quotient of a self-polar simplex stabilizer over $\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$ by the kernel of its projective monomial action on the unitary space spanned by the simplex lines, with $m\geq3$. Let $\bar A\leq\bar D$ be hereditarily $E$-permutable. Then $\bar A$ is normalized by the group $S_m$ acting by permutations of the coordinate lines.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
It suffices to show that a transposition $(ij)$ normalizes $\bar A$. As $m \geq 3$, choose a third coordinate $k$. On the three corresponding anisotropic lines take a monomial unitary element $w$. This element swaps the $i$-line and $j$-line, multiplies the $k$-line by $-1$, and fixes the remaining coordinate lines. In odd characteristic the swap has determinant $-1$ and the extra factor $-1$ restores determinant $1$. In characteristic $2$ the swap has determinant $1$. The element $w$ represents an element of the projective special unitary group with $w^2=1$ inducing $(ij)$.

In this paragraph, $E=\bar D\rtimes\langle w\rangle$ denotes the subgroup generated by $\bar D$ and $w$ inside $\bar D\rtimes S_m$. By hereditary permutability, $\bar A$ permutes with a conjugate of $\langle w\rangle$ in $E$. Write a generator of the chosen conjugate of $\langle w\rangle$ as $y=tw$ with $t\in\bar D$. Since $\bar A\langle y\rangle$ is a subgroup, for each $a\in\bar A$ the element $ya$ equals $a'y$ for some $a'\in\bar A$ (compare the nontrivial coset of $\bar D$ in $E/\bar D$). Therefore, $y\bar A y^{-1}=\bar A$. As $t\in\bar D$ centralizes the diagonal subgroup $\bar A$, we get $w\bar Aw^{-1}=\bar A$. Since coordinate transpositions generate $S_m$, this proves the lemma.

label: lem:unitary-rank-two-ratio-bound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-rank-two-ratio-bound}
In the notation of {\rm Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-weyl-normalization}}, represent an element of $\bar A$ on the coordinate lines by
$$
        \operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_m),~ \lambda_i^{Q+1}=1.
$$
If $Q\geq3$, then $(\lambda_i/\lambda_j)^4=1$ for every pair $i,j$.

title: Proof
body_md:
We fix $i
eq j$ and let $s=(ij)$, which normalizes $ ar A$ by Lemma ef{lem:unitary-weyl-normalization}. For $a\in ar A$ let $ ar c=a^{-1}a^s\in ar A$. On the unitary subspace of dimension two $U=L_i\perp L_j$, the image of $ ar c$ in $\operatorname{PGU}(U)$ is $\operatorname{diag}(\delta,\delta^{-1})$ with $\delta=\lambda_j\lambda_i^{-1}$. This image of $ ar c$ lies in $N=\operatorname{PSU}(U)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(Q)$ (using $\operatorname{PSU}_2(Q)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(Q)$ \cite[p. 66]{Wilson2009}), and the projective order of this image equals the multiplicative order of $\delta^2$.

Let $ ar A_U$ be the image of $ ar A$ in $\operatorname{PGU}(U)$. Let $J_U$ denote the stabilizer of the orthogonal decomposition $U\perp U^\perp$ used for the hereditary condition of $ ar{A}$. We restrict this condition to $J_U$. Let $K_U$ be the complementary unitary factor of $J_U$ on $U^\perp$, acting on $U^\perp$ and trivially on $U$. To study the action on $U$, we take the quotient $J_U/K_U$ and use its induced projective action $ho_U:J_U/K_U	o\operatorname{PGU}(U)$ on $U$. By Lemma ef{lem:quotient-inheritance}, the image $ ar A_U$ satisfies the hereditary permutability condition in the group $ho_U(J_U/K_U)$ acting on the space $U$ of dimension two. Applying Lemma ef{lem:normal-intersection-transfer} to $ ar A_U$ for $N\unlhd\operatorname{PGU}(U)$ shows that the subgroup $K= ar A_U\cap N$ is ordinary $N$-permutable. eq1$. Since $K$ lies in the diagonal torus of $\operatorname{PGU}(U)$ determined by the two coordinate lines, $K$ is abelian, hence proper in $N$. label: lem:unitary-rank-three-toral-collapse
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-rank-three-toral-collapse}
In the notation of {\rm Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-weyl-normalization}}, the projective image of $\bar A$ on the span of any three coordinate lines is trivial.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
If $Q=2$, then we consider each nontrivial subgroup of the projective diagonal torus of $\operatorname{PGU}_3(2)$. A direct computation in $\operatorname{PGU}_3(2)$ finds a cyclic subgroup $H$ for each chosen toral subgroup. For this $H$, no conjugate of $H$ permutes with that toral subgroup inside the group generated by $H$ and the toral subgroup (Appendix \ref{app:pgu3-2-toral-certificate}). Hence no such toral subgroup is hereditarily $\operatorname{PGU}_3(2)$-permutable, and the projective image of $\bar{A}$ on the span of the three coordinate lines is trivial. Therefore, we may assume that $Q\geq3$.

By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-rank-two-ratio-bound}, the projective image of $\bar A$ on the span of any three coordinate lines is a $2$-group. By \cite[p. 66]{Wilson2009}, for a unitary space of dimension three over $\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$,
$$
        \operatorname{PGU}_3(Q)/\operatorname{PSU}_3(Q)\cong C_{(3,Q+1)}
$$
(the quotient being trivial when $(3,Q+1)=1$), so the diagonal $2$-group acting on the three coordinates has trivial image in this quotient and lies in $\operatorname{PSU}_3(Q)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} the projective image of $\bar A$ on the span of the three coordinate lines is hereditarily $\operatorname{PSU}_3(Q)$-permutable in $\operatorname{PSU}_3(Q)$. Since this image is a diagonal $2$-group, it is proper. Hence the result for $\operatorname{PSU}_3$ in Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-low-bases} shows that this image on three coordinates is trivial.

label: prop:unitary-toral
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unitary-toral}
Let $A$ be a hereditarily permutable subgroup contained in the projective diagonal torus of a self-polar simplex stabilizer $\Delta=D:S_m$ over $\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$, with $m\geq3$. Then $A=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We let $\bar A\leq\bar D$ be the image of $A$ under the projective monomial action on the space spanned by the $m$ simplex lines. By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-weyl-normalization} the image $\bar A$ is normalized by $S_m$, and by Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-rank-three-toral-collapse} the projective image of $\bar A$ on the span of any three coordinate lines is trivial. Hence all coordinate ratios in $\bar A$ are trivial and $\bar A=1$. Projectively, $A=1$.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md: The diagonal group $\bar D$ being abelian does not by itself show that the group $S_m$ acting by permutations of the coordinate lines normalizes $\bar A$. We prove this normalization by testing hereditary permutability of $\bar A$ against the cyclic subgroup generated by $w$ inside $\bar D\rtimes\langle w\rangle$. The involution $w$ constructed in the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-weyl-normalization} swaps the two chosen coordinate lines. Since $\bar A$ is diagonal, the conjugation calculation in this semidirect product shows that $w$ normalizes $\bar A$.

label: lem:unitary-singer-line-orbit-stabilizer
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-singer-line-orbit-stabilizer}
Let $F=\mathbb{F}_Q$, $E=\mathbb{F}_{Q^u}$, and let $\lambda\in E^\times$ have prime order $s$ with $\operatorname{ord}_s(Q)=u$. If an $F$-linear map $T\in\operatorname{GL}_F(E)$ stabilizes every line $F\lambda^i$ for $0\leq i<s$, then $T$ is scalar over $F$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Write $T$ as a linearized polynomial $T(X)=\sum_{k=0}^{u-1}a_kX^{Q^k}$ with $a_k\in E$. The condition that $T$ stabilizes the line $F\lambda^m$ means that $T(\lambda^m)=c_m\lambda^m$ with $c_m\in F$, and since $\lambda^s=1$ the scalar $c_m$ depends only on $m\pmod s$. Dividing by $\lambda^m$, we have, for every $m\in\mathbb{Z}/s$,
$$
        \sum_{k=0}^{u-1}a_k\,\lambda^{me_k}=c_m,~ e_k:=Q^k-1\!\!\pmod s .
$$
If $e_j=e_k$ with $j<k$, then $Q^{k-j}\equiv1\pmod s$. This congruence, together with $\operatorname{ord}_s(Q)=u$, forces $u\mid k-j$. Therefore, the residues $e_0=0,e_1,\dots,e_{u-1}$ are pairwise distinct. We view each side of $\sum_{k=0}^{u-1}a_k\,\lambda^{me_k}=c_m$ as a function $\mathbb{Z}/s\to E$ and expand both functions in the characters $\chi_e\colon m\mapsto\lambda^{me}$ $(e\in\mathbb{Z}/s)$. Write $p=\operatorname{char}F$ and let $\mu_s$ be the group of $s$th roots of unity. Since $s\neq p$ and $\mu_s\subseteq E^\times$, these characters are linearly independent over $E$. The identity reads $\sum_k a_k\chi_{e_k}=c$, where $c$ is the function $m\mapsto c_m$ on $\mathbb{Z}/s$. The set of exponents with nonzero coefficients is $\Sigma:=\{e_k:a_k\neq0\}$.

We now use the Frobenius map $x\mapsto x^Q$ on the character identity $\sum_k a_k\chi_{e_k}=c$. Since $\chi_e^Q=\chi_{Qe}$ and each $c_m\in F$ satisfies $c_m^Q=c_m$, the character identity becomes $\sum_k a_k^Q\chi_{Qe_k}=c$. We compare the nonzero coefficients in the two expressions for $c$. In this comparison, character independence and $a_k^Q\neq0\iff a_k\neq0$ give $Q\Sigma=\Sigma$. Hence $\Sigma$ is a union of $\langle Q\rangle$-orbits on $\mathbb{Z}/s$. The subgroup $\langle Q\rangle\leq(\mathbb{Z}/s)^\times$ has order $u$ and acts freely on the nonzero residues, so each orbit on the residues different from $0$ has size $u$. But $\Sigma\setminus\{0\}\subseteq\{e_1,\dots,e_{u-1}\}$ has at most $u-1$ elements. This is too few to contain an entire orbit on the nonzero residues. Therefore, $\Sigma\subseteq\{0\}$, i.e.\ $a_k=0$ for all $k\geq1$. Finally $T(1)=a_0=c_0\in F$, so $T=a_0I$ is scalar over $F$.

label: prop:unitary-unipotent
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unitary-unipotent}
Let $G=\operatorname{PSU}_u(Q)$ with $Q=p^f$ and $u\geq3$ odd, $(u,Q)\neq(3,2)$. Suppose that $A<G$ is proper, nontrivial, and hereditarily $G$-permutable, is a $p$-subgroup, and fixes a nondegenerate line $L_0$ of the natural module pointwise. Then no such $A$ exists.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $L_0$ is nondegenerate, $V=L_0\perp L_0^\perp$ is an $A$-invariant orthogonal decomposition of $V$, and $A$ fixes $L_0$ pointwise. Hence each nonidentity element of $A$, being unipotent and acting as the identity on the direct summand $L_0$, has a Jordan block of size $1$ on the natural unitary module $V$.

Choose a primitive prime divisor $s$ of $Q^{2u}-1$. Since $u\geq3$ and $(u,Q)\neq(3,2)$, such a divisor exists by Zsigmondy's theorem \cite{Zsigmondy1892}. This prime satisfies $\operatorname{ord}_s(Q)=2u$ and $s\equiv1\pmod{2u}$. Let $R=\langle r\rangle$ be the subgroup of order $s$ in an irreducible unitary Singer torus of $G$ acting on the natural module $V$ \cite[Table 1, Main Theorem]{Bereczky2000}. Since $A$ is a $p$-group and $s\neq p$, we have $A\cap R=1$.

By hereditary $G$-permutability of $A$, we choose a conjugate of $R$, again written $R$, with $H=AR$ a subgroup. Since $A\cap R=1$, the action of $H$ on the cosets of $A$ has prime degree $s$ and $R$ is regular on these cosets. We let $C=\operatorname{Core}_H(A)$. Because $A$ is a $p$-group and $|R|=s$ is a prime distinct from $p$, $|H|=|A|\,s=p^a s$, so $H$ is solvable by Burnside's $p^aq^b$ theorem \cite[Theorem 3.10]{DixonMortimer1996}. In the coset action of $H/C$, a solvable transitive group of prime degree $s$ has a normal Sylow $s$-subgroup \cite[Theorem 3.5B]{DixonMortimer1996}, so $RC/C\unlhd H/C$. In particular the nonsolvable possibility does not occur, and only two cases remain.

\emph{$R\unlhd H$.} Let $y\in A$ have order $p$. If $y$ centralized $R$, then $y$ would lie in the centralizer of the element $r$. The element $r$ acts irreducibly on the natural module, and its centralizer consists of the transformations acting by multiplication in $\mathbb{F}_{Q^{2u}}$, identified with the natural module $V$ over $\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$. The unitary transformations in this centralizer form a torus of elements of norm one, a $p'$-group \cite[Table 1]{Bereczky2000}. Hence $y$ acts nontrivially on $R$,
$$
        yry^{-1}=r^a,~ a\in(\mathbb{Z}/s\mathbb{Z})^\times,~ |a|=p.
$$
The eigenvalues of $r$ form one orbit under the map $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{-Q}$,
$$
        \lambda,\lambda^{-Q},\ldots,\lambda^{(-Q)^{u-1}},
$$
and the eigenvalue multiset of $r^a$ must equal the eigenvalue multiset of $r$. So exponentiation by $a$ sends $\lambda$ into the $\langle -Q\rangle$-orbit of $\lambda$, and unitary semisimple conjugacy forces
$$
        a\in\langle -Q\rangle,~ |\langle -Q\rangle|=u.
$$
Equivalently, $N_G(R)/C_G(R)$ is cyclic of order $u$, generated by the map on eigenvalues $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{-Q}$ \cite[Main Theorem]{Bereczky2000}. Since the central scalars lie in $C_G(R)$, taking the quotient of $\operatorname{SU}_u(Q)$ by $Z(\operatorname{SU}_u(Q))$ to obtain $\operatorname{PSU}_u(Q)$ leaves $N_G(R)/C_G(R)$ cyclic of order $u$ in the projective group $G$, with generator induced by the map on eigenvalues $\lambda\mapsto\lambda^{-Q}$. Therefore, the automorphism induced by $y$ on $R$ lies in $\langle -Q\rangle$. As $|a|=p$ and $\langle -Q\rangle$ is cyclic of order $u$, we have $p\mid u$. If $p\nmid u$, then there is no element $a$ of order $p$ in $\langle -Q\rangle$, so $R\not\unlhd H$. The element $y$ permutes the eigenlines of $r$ in cycles of length $p$. On the span of each cycle the matrix of $y$ is a cyclic permutation matrix. In characteristic $p$ this matrix is a single Jordan block of size $p$, not of size $1$. So $y$ has no Jordan block of size $1$, contradicting the fact that $A$ fixes $L_0$ pointwise. Hence $R\not\unlhd H$.

\emph{$RC/C\unlhd H/C$ but $R\not\unlhd H$.} Since $H=AR$, the core of $A$ in $H$ is
$$
        C=\bigcap_{i=0}^{s-1}A^{r^i}.
$$
As $A$ fixes the line $L_0$, the subgroup $C$ stabilizes every line in the $R$-orbit $L_0,L_0^r,\ldots,L_0^{r^{s-1}}$. By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-singer-line-orbit-stabilizer} (with $Q$ replaced by $Q^2$, so its fields are $F=\mathbb{F}_{Q^2}$ and $E=\mathbb{F}_{Q^{2u}}$), $C$ is scalar on the natural module $V$. But $C\leq A$ is a $p$-group, while the scalars are elements of norm one of $p'$-order. Therefore, $C=1$. Then $RC/C\unlhd H/C$ implies that $R\unlhd H$. But $R\unlhd H$ is incompatible with the Jordan blocks forced by the fixed line $L_0$. Both cases are impossible, so no such $A$ exists.

label: lem:unitary-unipotent-root-sl2
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-unipotent-root-sl2}
Let $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ with $n\geq3$ and $q\geq3$, and let $A<G$ be proper, nontrivial, and hereditarily $G$-permutable. If $A$ is contained in a single subgroup $T_{\langle v\rangle}=\{\,x\mapsto x+\lambda\langle x,v\rangle v:\lambda^q=-\lambda\,\}$ corresponding to a long root ($v$ isotropic), then $A=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We choose $w$ so that the space $\langle v,w\rangle$ spanned by $v$ and $w$ is a hyperbolic plane and let $R=\langle T_{\langle v\rangle},T_{\langle w\rangle}\rangle\cong\operatorname{SU}_2(q)\cong\operatorname{SL}_2(q)$ \cite[p.~66]{Wilson2009}, so $Z(R)=\{\pm I\}$. A nonidentity element of $T_{\langle v\rangle}$ is unipotent, hence not $-I$, so $A\cap Z(R)=1$. By Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} ($A\leq R\leq G$) and Lemma \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance} (modulo $Z(R)$), the image $\bar A$ of $A$ in $R/Z(R)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ is hereditarily $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$-permutable and isomorphic to $A$. The subgroup $\bar A$ lies in the image of $T_{\langle v\rangle}$ in $R/Z(R)$, a point stabilizer (Borel subgroup) of $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$. Since $q\geq3$, we have $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)\not\cong\operatorname{PGL}_2(2)$, so Lemma \ref{lem:pgl2-borel} shows that $\bar A=1$. Hence $A=1$.

label: lem:unitary-extension-quotient
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-extension-quotient}
Let $n=ub$ with $b$ an odd prime, and let
$$
        E_b=N_G(S_b),~ S_b\cong\operatorname{PSU}_u(q^b),~ G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q).
$$
Then every prime divisor of $|E_b/S_b|$ divides $b(q^b+1)/(q+1)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The normalizer $E_b=N_G(S_b)$ comes from the subgroup in class $\mathcal C_3$ of Kleidman and Liebeck \cite[\S4.3, Table 4.3.A]{KleidmanLiebeck1990} that fixes an extension field structure as a whole. This structure comes from $\operatorname{GU}_u(q^b)$ inside $\operatorname{GU}_n(q)$, with the natural space viewed over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{2b}}$. If $\delta\in C_{q^b+1}$ is the determinant over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{2b}}$, then the determinant over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ is
$$
        N_{\mathbb{F}_{q^{2b}}/\mathbb{F}_{q^2}}(\delta)=\delta^{1+q^2+\cdots+q^{2(b-1)}}.
$$
Set $M=q^b+1$ and $N=1+q^2+\cdots+q^{2(b-1)}$. Since $b$ is odd,
$$
        N=\frac{q^{2b}-1}{q^2-1}=\frac{q^b-1}{q-1}\cdot\frac{q^b+1}{q+1}.
$$
Since $1+q+\cdots+q^{b-1}\equiv1\pmod{q+1}$, we have $\gcd(q+1,(q^b-1)/(q-1))=1$. Hence $\gcd(M,N)=(q^b+1)/(q+1)$, so the norm kernel on $C_{q^b+1}$ has order $(q^b+1)/(q+1)$. The special unitary determinant condition restricts $\delta$ to this norm kernel and removes the $(q+1)$-part. The automorphism of the extension $\mathbb{F}_{q^{2b}}/\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ contributes only the factor $b$. Passing from $\operatorname{SU}_n(q)$ to $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ means taking the quotient by $Z(\operatorname{SU}_n(q))$, which cannot introduce new prime divisors. Therefore, every prime divisor of $|E_b/S_b|$ divides $b(q^b+1)/(q+1)$.

label: lem:unitary-visibility-gcd
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-visibility-gcd}
If $b\nmid q+1$, then
$$
        \gcd\!\left(b\,\frac{q^b+1}{q+1},\,q+1\right)=1.
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $b\nmid q+1$, we have $(b,q+1)=1$, and
$$
        \frac{q^b+1}{q+1}=q^{b-1}-q^{b-2}+\cdots-q+1\equiv b\pmod{q+1}.
$$
A common prime divisor of the integers $b(q^b+1)/(q+1)$ and $q+1$ would divide $b$, but no prime divisor of $b$ divides $q+1$.

label: lem:unitary-alt-transfer
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-alt-transfer}
Let $m\geq7$ and let $B\leq S_m$ be hereditarily $S_m$-permutable. Then $K=B\cap A_m$ is ordinary $A_m$-permutable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $C\leq A_m$. Hereditary $S_m$-permutability of $B$ ensures that $BC^x=C^xB$ for some $x\in\langle B,C\rangle$. If $x\in A_m$, then we use $x$ itself as the conjugating element. If $x\notin A_m$, then $B\not\leq A_m$ (else $\langle B,C\rangle\leq A_m$). We pick $b\in B\setminus A_m$ and set $a=xb\in A_m$. Conjugating $BC^x$ by $b$ produces $BC^a$, and since $C^a\leq A_m$,
$$
        (BC^a)\cap A_m=(B\cap A_m)C^a=KC^a
$$
is a subgroup, so $KC^a=C^aK$. Since $C\leq A_m$ was arbitrary, $K$ is ordinary $A_m$-permutable.

label: lem:unitary-subset
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-subset}
Let $B\leq S_m$ be hereditarily $S_m$-permutable, and let $H=S_k\times S_{m-k}$ be the setwise stabilizer in $S_m$ of a subset of size $k$ with $1\leq k<m/2$. Then either $B\leq H^x$ for some $x$, or $S_m=BH^x$ for some $x$. In the factorization case $S_m=BH^x$, the group $B$ is transitive on $k$-subsets and $\binom{m}{k}\mid|B|$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We use Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} in $S_m$ for the maximal subgroup $H$. The factorization $S_m=BH^x$ makes $B$ transitive on the cosets of $H$, i.e., on $k$-subsets.

label: lem:no-solvable-four-homogeneous
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:no-solvable-four-homogeneous}
For $N\geq8$ no solvable subgroup of $S_N$ is $4$-homogeneous.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $B\leq S_N$ be $4$-homogeneous with $N\geq8$, so that $4\leq N/2$. By the Livingstone and Wagner theorem \cite[Theorem 2]{LivingstoneWagner1965}, we have that $B$ is $3$-transitive, in particular $2$-transitive and primitive. If $B$ is $4$-transitive, then by the classification of the multiply transitive groups \cite[\S7.4]{DixonMortimer1996}, $B$ is alternating, symmetric, or one of the Mathieu groups $M_{11},M_{12},M_{23},M_{24}$. If $B$ is $4$-homogeneous but not $4$-transitive, then by Kantor's classification of such groups \cite[Theorem 1]{Kantor1972}, $B$ is $\operatorname{PGL}_2(8)$ or $\operatorname{P\Gamma L}_2(8)$ of degree $9$, or $\operatorname{P\Gamma L}_2(32)$ of degree $33$. Every entry of both lists contains a nonabelian simple group (an alternating group $A_N$ with $N\geq 8$, a Mathieu group, or $\operatorname{PSL}_2(8)$ or $\operatorname{PSL}_2(32)$), so $B$ is nonsolvable. Hence no solvable subgroup of $S_N$ is $4$-homogeneous.

label: lem:solvable-simplex-prime-bound
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:solvable-simplex-prime-bound}
Let $N\geq5$ be odd and let $B\leq S_N$ be solvable and hereditarily $S_N$-permutable. Then $B$ stabilizes a partition of the $N$ points into parts of size $4$ together with one part of size $5$ or $7$. $B$ acts trivially on the part of size $5$ or $7$. Every prime divisor of $|B|$ is $2$ or $3$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We induct on the odd integer $N$. If $N\in\{5,7\}$, then Lemma \ref{lem:s5-no-solvable-hereditary} for $N=5$ and Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-solvable-high-prime-simplex} for $N=7$ (with $u=7$) show that $B=1$. We take the whole set of $N$ points as the single part of the partition. This partition satisfies the conclusion.

We let $N\geq9$ be odd. Since $B$ is solvable and $N\geq8$, Lemma \ref{lem:no-solvable-four-homogeneous} shows that $B$ is not $4$-homogeneous. As $4<N/2$, the setwise stabilizer $H=S_4\times S_{N-4}$ of a subset of size $4$ is maximal in $S_N$. The product alternative $S_N = BH^x$ of Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-subset} would make $B$ transitive on $4$-sets and hence $4$-homogeneous. Therefore, this product alternative cannot occur. Hence $B\leq H^x$ for some $x$, i.e., $B$ stabilizes a subset $S_0$ of size $4$. Then $B\leq S_{S_0}\times S_{\Omega}$ with $\Omega$ the complementary $(N-4)$-set. We restrict hereditary permutability of $B$ from $S_N$ to $S_{S_0}\times S_{\Omega}$ (Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction}). To obtain the action on $\Omega$, we take the quotient of the symmetric group $S_{S_0} \times S_{\Omega}$ by its direct factor $S_{S_0}$, which acts on $S_0$ and fixes $\Omega$ pointwise (Lemma \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance}). Therefore, the image $B'$ of $B$ in $S_\Omega$ is solvable and hereditarily $S_{N-4}$-permutable. As $N-4\geq5$ is odd, induction shows that $B'$ stabilizes a partition of $\Omega$ into parts of size $4$ and one part of size $5$ or $7$. Moreover, $B'$ acts trivially on the part of size $5$ or $7$. Induction also shows that $|B'|$ is divisible by no prime other than $2$ or $3$. Adjoining $S_0$ produces the partition of all $N$ points, with the same part of size $5$ or $7$ as in the partition of $\Omega$. Because the action of $B$ on $\Omega$ factors through $B'$, $B$ acts trivially on the part of size $5$ or $7$. Finally the kernel of $B\to B'$ is supported on $S_0$, hence lies in $S_{S_0}\cong S_4$, a $\{2,3\}$-group, and $|B'|$ is a $\{2,3\}$-number, so $|B|$ is a $\{2,3\}$-number.

label: lem:unitary-solvable-low-socle-simplex
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-solvable-low-socle-simplex}
Let $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ with $n=ub$ odd, where $b$ is an odd prime with $b\nmid q+1$ and $u\geq3$. Let $E=N_G(S)$ with $S\cong\operatorname{PSU}_u(q^b)$ be the normalizer in $G$ of the subgroup defined by the extension field $\mathbb{F}_{q^{2b}}$. Suppose that a hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup $A$ lies in $E$ and in a self-polar simplex stabilizer $\Delta=D:S_n$. If the image of $A$ in $E/S$ is nontrivial and the permutation image $B=AD/D$ of $A$ on the simplex lines is solvable, then no such subgroup $A$ exists.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We write $Q=AS/S\neq1$ for the nontrivial image of $A$ in the quotient $E/S$ of the extension field normalizer $E$ by its socle $S$. The permutation image $B=AD/D$ of $A$ on the simplex lines is hereditarily $S_n$-permutable (Lemmas \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} and \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance}). By hypothesis $B$ is solvable, and $n=ub$ is odd with $n\geq9$, so Lemma \ref{lem:symmetric-solvable-hereditary-trivial} shows that $B=1$. Hence $A$ lies in the diagonal torus $D$ in $G$, and Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-toral} shows that $A=1$. But then $Q=AS/S=1$, contradicting $Q\neq1$. So no such subgroup $A$ exists.

label: lem:unitary-transitive-alternating
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-transitive-alternating}
Let $d\geq7$ and let $C\leq S_d$ be nonsolvable, transitive, and hereditarily $S_d$-permutable. Then $C\geq A_d$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $1\leq k<d/2$ let $H_k=S_k\times S_{d-k}$ be the setwise stabilizer in $S_d$ of a subset of size $k$. As $C$ is transitive, the group $C$ lies in no conjugate of $H_k$. Therefore, the product alternative $S_d = CH_k ^x$ of Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-subset} holds and $C$ is $k$-homogeneous for each such $k$. In particular, $C$ is $h$-homogeneous with $h=\lfloor(d-1)/2\rfloor\geq3$, hence $2$-transitive and primitive \cite[Theorem 2]{LivingstoneWagner1965}.

A $5$-homogeneous group is $5$-transitive \cite[Theorem 2]{LivingstoneWagner1965}, and by the classification of multiply transitive groups \cite[\S7.4]{DixonMortimer1996}, the $5$-transitive groups of degree $\neq12,24$ are alternating or symmetric. If $d\geq13$, then $h\geq6$, so $C$ is $6$-transitive and $C\geq A_d$. If $d=11$, then $h\geq5$, so $C$ is $5$-transitive of degree $11$ and $C\geq A_{11}$.

If $d=12$, then $h=5$, so $C$ is $5$-transitive of degree $12$, and the $5$-transitive groups of degree $12$ are $A_{12}$, $S_{12}$, and the Mathieu group $M_{12}$ \cite[\S7.4]{DixonMortimer1996}. Since $ C$ is $2$-transitive, the group $C$ is primitive and lies in no conjugate of the imprimitive maximal subgroup $H=S_6\wr S_2$. By Lemmas \ref{lem:maximal-product} and \ref{lem:factorization-coset-transitivity} the index $[S_{12}:H]=\tfrac12\binom{12}{6}=462=2\cdot3\cdot7\cdot11$ divides $|C|$. Since $|M_{12}|=95040=2^6\cdot3^3\cdot5\cdot11$ is not divisible by $7$, the divisibility condition shows that $C$ cannot be $M_{12}$, so $C\geq A_{12}$. The normalizer in $S_{12}$ of this copy of $M_{12}$ acting on twelve points is $M_{12}$ itself. The outer automorphism of $M_{12}$ is not induced by a permutation of the twelve points.

For $8\leq d\leq10$ we use Jordan's theorem. A primitive subgroup of $S_d$ containing a $p$-cycle for a prime $p\leq d-3$ contains $A_d$ \cite[Theorem 3.3E]{DixonMortimer1996}. Being primitive, $C$ lies in no conjugate of an imprimitive maximal subgroup $M$, so by Lemmas \ref{lem:maximal-product} and \ref{lem:factorization-coset-transitivity} the index $[S_d:M]$ divides $|C|$. Taking $M=S_4\wr S_2<S_8$, $M=S_3\wr S_3<S_9$, and $M=S_5\wr S_2<S_{10}$ produces indices $35$, $280$, and $126$ respectively, providing the prime $5$ (for $d=8,9$) or $7$ (for $d=10$) as a divisor of $|C|$. In each case $d/2<p\leq d-3$, so an element of the indicated prime order in $C$ is a single $p$-cycle and Jordan's theorem shows that $C\geq A_d$.

For $d=7$ the nonsolvable transitive groups are $\operatorname{PSL}_3(2),A_7,S_7$ \cite[Table 7A]{ButlerMcKay1983}. Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-subset} for $3$-subsets forces $\binom{7}{3}=35\mid|C|$, incompatible with $|\operatorname{PSL}_3(2)|=168$, so $C\geq A_7$. In every case $C\geq A_d$.

label: lem:alternating-permutation-no-two
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:alternating-permutation-no-two}
Let $F$ be a field and let $d\geq5$. The natural permutation module $V=F^d$ for $A_d$ has no $2$-dimensional $A_d$-submodule.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let
$$
        \mathbf 1=e_1+\cdots+e_d,
        ~ T=F\mathbf 1,
        ~ W=\left\{\sum a_i e_i:\sum a_i=0\right\}.
$$
We first consider vectors of minimal support. Let $0\neq Y\leq W$ be an $A_d$-submodule, and suppose that $Y$ is not contained in $T$. We choose $y=(a_1,\ldots,a_d)\in Y\setminus T$. Since $y$ is not constant, two coordinates differ, say $a_i\neq a_j$. Choose $k$ distinct from $i,j$ and set $z=y-y^{(ijk)}$. Then $0\neq z\in Y$ and $z$ is supported on at most three coordinates. If $z$ has support two, then $z$ is a scalar multiple of some $e_r-e_s$. Suppose that $z$ has support three, say on $\{r,s,t\}$. If two nonzero coefficients (say those at $r$ and $s$) differ, then choose two points $a,b$ outside the support of $z$ and act on $z$ by $(rs)(ab)$. The difference $z-z^{(rs)(ab)}$ is a nonzero vector of $Y$ supported on $\{r,s\}$. If the three nonzero coefficients are all equal, then the characteristic is $3$. Choosing a point $a$ outside the support of $z$ and acting on $z$ by $(rs)(ta)$ produces a difference equal to a scalar multiple of $e_t-e_a$. Thus, in all cases $Y$ contains $e_r-e_s$ for some $r\neq s$. Since $A_d$ is $2$-transitive for $d\geq5$, the $A_d$-orbit of $e_r-e_s$ spans $W$. Hence $Y=W$.

Now suppose that $X\leq V$ is an $A_d$-submodule of dimension $2$. If $X\leq W$, then the argument using vectors of minimal support for submodules of $W$ shows that either $X\leq T$ or $X=W$, both impossible. Hence $X\nleq W$, and $X\cap W$ is an invariant line. By the argument using vectors of minimal support for submodules of $W$, the line $X\cap W$ must be $T$. In particular the characteristic divides $d$, so that $T\leq W$. The quotient $X/T$ embeds in the trivial module $V/W$, and $T$ is also trivial. Since $A_d$ is perfect for $d\geq5$, the action of $A_d$ on the extension $X$ of $X/T$ by $T$ is trivial. The space $X$ is fixed pointwise by $A_d$, but since $A_d$ is transitive, the fixed space of $A_d$ on $V$ is exactly $T$, of dimension $1$. This contradiction proves the lemma.

label: lem:unitary-full-support-simplex
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-full-support-simplex}
Let $\operatorname{PSU}_d(Q)\leq E\leq\operatorname{PGU}_d(Q)$ with $Q=p^f$ and $d\geq5$, let $\Delta=D:S_d$ be a self-polar simplex stabilizer in $E$, and suppose that $A\leq\Delta$ is hereditarily $E$-permutable with $B=AD/D\geq A_d$. Then no such $A$ exists.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $P_1$ be the stabilizer in $E$ of a totally singular $1$-space in the natural unitary module of $E$. Let $P_2$ be the stabilizer in $E$ of a totally singular $2$-space in the natural unitary module of $E$. Since $d\geq5$, the Witt index of this unitary module is at least $2$, so both subspaces exist and $P_1,P_2$ are maximal parabolics in ${\rm PGU}_d (Q)$. The maximality of these parabolic subgroups is the usual maximality of maximal parabolics in the finite $BN$-pair. The unitary stabilizers of these totally singular subspaces are listed in Kleidman and Liebeck \cite[Table 3.5.B]{KleidmanLiebeck1990}, and the Levi quotients of $P_1$ and $P_2$ are those of \cite[Proposition 26.1(b)]{MalleTesterman2011}. Since $\operatorname{PSU}_d(Q)$ is transitive on totally singular $i$-subspaces and each stabilizer $P_i$ maps onto $E/\operatorname{PSU}_d(Q)$, the maximality of $P_i$ holds in every intermediate group $E$.

Every prime divisor of $|D|$ divides $Q+1$, and every prime divisor of $|S_d|$ is at most $d$. Since $A\leq\Delta=D:S_d$, it is enough, for each $i=1,2$, to find a prime $r\mid[E:P_i]$ with $r>d$ and $r\nmid Q+1$. Then $[E:P_i]\nmid |A|$, so the product alternative $E=AP_i^x$ in Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} cannot occur and $A$ lies in a conjugate of $P_i$. 

The indices of $P_1$ and $P_2$ in $E$ are the numbers of totally singular $1$-spaces and $2$-spaces in this natural unitary module,
$$
        [E:P_1]=\frac{(Q^d-(-1)^d)(Q^{d-1}-(-1)^{d-1})}{Q^2-1},
$$
$$
        [E:P_2]=\frac{(Q^d-(-1)^d)(Q^{d-1}-(-1)^{d-1})(Q^{d-2}-(-1)^{d-2})(Q^{d-3}-(-1)^{d-3})}{(Q^4-1)(Q^2-1)}.
$$
Zsigmondy's theorem \cite{Zsigmondy1892} provides the primitive prime divisors in the following two cases. If $d$ is odd, then take a primitive prime divisor $r$ of $Q^{2d}-1$. Then $\operatorname{ord}_r(Q)=2d$, so $r\mid Q^d+1=Q^d-(-1)^d$. As $2d>4$, $r$ divides  neither $Q^2-1$ nor $Q^4-1$, and $r\equiv1\pmod{2d}$ implies that $r>d$ and $r\nmid Q+1$. If $d$ is even and $(Q,d)\neq(2,6)$, then take a primitive prime divisor $r$ of $Q^d-1$. Then $\operatorname{ord}_r(Q)=d$, so $r\mid Q^d-1=Q^d-(-1)^d$. As $d>4$, $r$ divides neither $Q^2-1$ nor $Q^4-1$, and $r\equiv1\pmod d$ implies that $r>d$ and $r\nmid Q+1$. For the exceptional pair $(Q,d)=(2,6)$ the factor $Q^{d-1}-(-1)^{d-1}=2^5+1=33$ contributes $r=11$, which divides $[E:P_1]=693$ and $[E:P_2]=6237$ but neither $Q+1=3$ nor $6!$. In each case, a prime $r>d$ with $r\nmid Q+1$ divides both $[E:P_1]$ and $[E:P_2]$. Hence $A\leq P_1^x$ and $A\leq P_2^y$, so $A$ stabilizes a totally singular $1$-space $\ell=\langle v\rangle$ and a totally singular $2$-space $U$.

We let $A^+\leq A$ be the preimage of $A_d\leq B$ under the permutation homomorphism from $A$ to $B=AD/D$ on the simplex lines. Since $A_d$ is transitive on the $d$ simplex coordinates, the vector $v$ has full support, $v=(v_1,\dots,v_d)$ with all $v_i\neq0$. To describe the projective action, conjugate the monomial group by $T=\operatorname{diag}(v_1,\dots,v_d)$, using the map $g\mapsto T^{-1}gT$. An element $g=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_d)P_\sigma$ of $A^+$ stabilizes $\ell=\langle v\rangle$, so $gv=\mu_gv$ for a scalar $\mu_g$. After conjugation by $T$ the element $g$ becomes $\mu_gP_\sigma$, so the projective action of $A^+$ is the ordinary permutation action of $A_d$ on the $d$-point permutation module $(\mathbb{F}_{Q^2})^d$, with $A_d$ permuting its coordinate vectors. The invariant $2$-space $U$ then produces a $2$-dimensional $A_d$-submodule $T^{-1}U$ of the $d$-point permutation module for $A_d$, contradicting Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-permutation-no-two}. This contradiction shows that no such $A$ exists.

label: lem:unitary-small-simplex
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-small-simplex}
Let $\operatorname{PSU}_d(Q)\leq E\leq\operatorname{PGU}_d(Q)$ with $d\in\{5,6\}$ and $Q=p^f$, let $\Delta=D:S_d$ be a self-polar simplex stabilizer in $E$, and suppose that $A\leq\Delta$ is hereditarily $E$-permutable with $B=AD/D$ nonsolvable and transitive on the $d$ lines of the simplex. Then no such $A$ exists.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Lemmas \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} and \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance}, $B$ is hereditarily $S_d$-permutable. By Butler and McKay \cite{ButlerMcKay1983}, the nonsolvable transitive groups of degree $5$ are $A_5,S_5$. In degree $6$, they are $A_6,S_6$ together with the actions of degree six of $A_5\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(5)$ and $S_5\cong\operatorname{PGL}_2(5)$.

If $B\geq A_d$, then Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-full-support-simplex}, which is valid for all $d\geq5$, contradicts the assumed existence of $A$. This settles degree $5$, where $A_5$ and $S_5$ both contain $A_5$, and the cases $A_6,S_6$ in degree $6$.

We now consider the remaining case $d=6$ with $B\in\{A_5,S_5\}$. In their transitive actions of degree six $A_5\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(5)$ and $S_5\cong\operatorname{PGL}_2(5)$ act on the projective line over $\mathbb{F}_5$, where no nonidentity element fixes more than two of the six points. In particular neither of these transitive groups of degree six contains a transposition. Let $t\in S_6$ be a transposition. By Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} the hereditarily $S_d$-permutable group $B$ permutes with a conjugate $\langle t^x\rangle$, so $P=B\langle t^x\rangle$ is a subgroup containing the transposition $t^x$. If $B=A_5$, then $t^x\notin B$ implies that $|P|=120$. In this case, $P$ contains the transitive group $A_5$, so the subgroup $P$ is transitive. The transitive subgroups of $S_6$ of order $120$ are the copies of $\operatorname{PGL}_2(5)$, none containing a transposition, a contradiction. If $B=S_5$, then $t^x\notin B$ implies that $|P|=240$. In this case, the subgroup would have index $3$ in $S_6$, but no subgroup of that index exists. Both remaining possibilities for $B$ are impossible.
