label: lem:symmetric-odd-involution-not-hereditary
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:symmetric-odd-involution-not-hereditary}
Let $u>5$ be an odd prime. No subgroup of $S_u$ generated by an odd involution is hereditarily $S_u$-permutable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $B=\langle \tau\rangle$ with $\tau$ an odd involution, written as a product of $t$ transpositions, and let $f=u-2t$ be its number of fixed points. Since $\tau$ is odd, $t$ is odd. The integer $u$ is also odd, so $f$ is odd. Consequently, $f=1$ or $f\geq3$.

Suppose that $f\geq3$. Choose a transposition $(ab)$ of $\tau$ and three fixed points $c,d,e$, and let $h=(abcde)$ and $H=\langle h\rangle$. On $\{a,b,c,d,e\}$ the transposition $(ab)$ and the $5$-cycle $h$ generate $S_5$. The remaining transpositions of $\tau$ are disjoint from $\{a,b,c,d,e\}$. Both $\tau$ and $h$ map $\{a,b,c,d,e\}$ to itself, and the restriction of $\tau$ to this set is $(ab)$. If $B$ were hereditarily $S_u$-permutable, then for some $x\in\langle B,H\rangle$ the product $BH^x$ would be a subgroup. As $|B|=2$ and $|H^x|=5$ are coprime, $|BH^x|=10$ and $H^x\unlhd BH^x$, so $\tau$ normalizes $H^x$. Since $\langle B,H\rangle$ maps $\{a,b,c,d,e\}$ to itself, restriction to this set of five points shows that $(ab)$ normalizes a group generated by a $5$-cycle. In $N_{S_5}(\langle (abcde)\rangle)\cong\operatorname{AGL}_1(5)$ every involution has cycle type $(2,2,1)$, whereas $(ab)$ has cycle type $(2,1,1,1)$, so this normalization is impossible.

The remaining case is $f=1$, where $t=(u-1)/2\geq3$, so $\tau$ has two transpositions $(ab)$ and $(cd)$. Let $h=(bc)$ and $H=\langle h\rangle$. On $\{a,b,c,d\}$,
$$
        \langle (ab)(cd),(bc)\rangle\cong D_8,
$$
and in this dihedral group the conjugates of $(bc)$ are $(bc)$ and $(ad)$, neither of which commutes with $(ab)(cd)$. Since $\langle B,H\rangle$ maps $\{a,b,c,d\}$ to itself and $h$ is supported on that set of four points, every $\langle B,H\rangle$-conjugate of $h$ is supported in $\{a,b,c,d\}$, hence equals $(bc)$ or $(ad)$. As the remaining transpositions of $\tau$ are disjoint from $\{a,b,c,d\}$, such a conjugate commutes with $\tau$ if and only if the conjugate commutes with $(ab)(cd)$. Neither of the two conjugates commutes with this double transposition. As two subgroups of order $2$ permute if and only if their generators commute, no conjugate of $H$ permutes with $B$, contradicting hereditary $S_u$-permutability of $B$.

label: lem:symmetric-three-cycle-not-hereditary
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:symmetric-three-cycle-not-hereditary}
Let $N\geq5$. No subgroup of $S_N$ generated by a single $3$-cycle is hereditarily $S_N$-permutable.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $B=\langle (a\,b\,c)\rangle$, and choose two further points $d,e$. We let $h=(a\,b\,c\,d\,e)$ and $H=\langle h\rangle$. On $\{a,b,c,d,e\}$ the $3$-cycle and the $5$-cycle generate $A_5$ (any subgroup of $A_5$ of order divisible by $15$ is $A_5$), and both fix the remaining $N-5$ points. So $\langle B,H\rangle$ acts as $A_5$ on $\{a,b,c,d,e\}$ and trivially elsewhere. If $B$ were hereditarily $S_N$-permutable, then since $|B|=3$ and $|H|=5$ are coprime, we could choose some $x\in\langle B,H\rangle$ such that $BH^x$ is a subgroup of order $|B|\,|H|/|B\cap H^x|=15$. But a subgroup of order $15$ would be cyclic, with an element of order $15$, which $A_5$ lacks. The group $A_5$ has no such subgroup. Hence no conjugate of $H$ permutes with $B$, contradicting hereditary $S_N$-permutability of $B$.

label: lem:unitary-solvable-high-prime-simplex
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-solvable-high-prime-simplex}
Let $u>5$ be prime and let $B\leq S_u$ be solvable and hereditarily $S_u$-permutable. Then $B=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $K=B\cap A_u$. By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-alt-transfer}, $K$ is ordinary $A_u$-permutable. Since $B$ is solvable, $K<A_u$. Therefore, the theorem of Yang and Galt \cite[Theorem 2]{YG2023} shows that $K=1$. Hence $B\hookrightarrow S_u/A_u\cong C_2$. If $B\cong C_2$, then $B$ is generated by an odd involution of $S_u$, contradicting Lemma \ref{lem:symmetric-odd-involution-not-hereditary}. Therefore, $B=1$.

label: lem:symmetric-solvable-hereditary-trivial
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:symmetric-solvable-hereditary-trivial}
For every odd $N\geq5$, the symmetric group $S_N$ has no nontrivial solvable hereditarily $S_N$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: We induct on the odd integer $N$. For $N=5$, we use Lemma \ref{lem:s5-no-solvable-hereditary} and for $N=7$ Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-solvable-high-prime-simplex}. Let $N\geq9$ and let $B\leq S_N$ be solvable and hereditarily $S_N$-permutable. Since $B$ is solvable and $N\geq8$, Lemma \ref{lem:no-solvable-four-homogeneous} shows that $B$ is not $4$-homogeneous, so by Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-subset} (with $k=4<N/2$) $B$ stabilizes a subset $S_0$ of size $4$. Let $\Omega$ be the complementary $(N-4)$-set. We restrict hereditary permutability of $B$ in $S_N$ to $\operatorname{Stab}_{S_N}(S_0)=\operatorname{Sym}(S_0)\times\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega)$. For the induced action on $\Omega$, we take the quotient of this direct product by $\operatorname{Sym}(S_0)$, the kernel of its action on $\Omega$ (Lemmas \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} and \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance}). Therefore, the image of $B$ in $\operatorname{Sym}(\Omega)\cong S_{N-4}$ is solvable and hereditarily $S_{N-4}$-permutable. As $N-4\geq5$ is odd, the image of $B$ on $\Omega$ is trivial by induction. Hence $B$ acts trivially on $\Omega$, i.e., $B\leq\operatorname{Sym}(S_0)\cong S_4$ and $B$ fixes $\Omega$ pointwise. For each nontrivial subgroup of this copy of $S_4$, the computation of Appendix \ref{app:degree-nine-base} finds a $5$-cycle or $7$-cycle $h$ on $S_0$ together with two or three points of $\Omega$. Let $H=\langle h\rangle$. For this chosen cyclic subgroup, no $x\in\langle B,H\rangle$ makes $BH^x$ a subgroup. Since $\langle B,H\rangle$ is then supported on at most seven points, the same failure of permutability occurs inside the copy of $S_7$ on those points, adjoining fixed points when fewer than seven points are used, and is independent of $N$. Therefore, no nontrivial subgroup of this copy of $S_4$ is hereditarily permutable in the symmetric group $S_N$, and $B=1$.

label: thm:unitary-simplex-image
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unitary-simplex-image}
Let $A\leq D:S_m$ be a hereditarily $E$-permutable  subgroup  with $\operatorname{PSU}_m(Q)\leq E\leq\operatorname{PGU}_m(Q)$, and let $B=AD/D\leq S_m$. Then $B=1$, and the remaining case of a subgroup of the diagonal torus $D$ in $E$ is settled by {\rm Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-toral}}.
head: environment
name: Permutation images on the lines of a self-polar simplex

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $m$ be the number of simplex lines and $Q$ the value used in the unitary group notation. The simplex stabilizer lies in a group $E$ with $\operatorname{PSU}_m(Q)\leq E\leq\operatorname{PGU}_m(Q)$. The subgroup $A$ is hereditarily $E$-permutable. Suppose that $B$ is solvable. By Lemmas \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} and \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance} the image $B$ is hereditarily $S_m$-permutable. In the descent for unitary groups of odd dimension, the number $m$ of simplex lines is the dimension of the unitary space, so $m$ is odd and $m\geq5$. Hence $B=1$ by Lemma \ref{lem:symmetric-solvable-hereditary-trivial}.

Suppose that $B$ is nonsolvable. As $B$ embeds in the product of the permutation images of $B$ on its orbits, not all of these permutation images are solvable. Therefore, we choose a $B$-orbit $\Omega$ with $C=B^\Omega$ nonsolvable, and let $d=|\Omega|$. Since $B$ maps $\Omega$ to itself, the group $B$ lies in $S_\Omega\times S_{\Omega^c}$. We restrict the hereditary condition of $B$ in $S_m$ to $S_\Omega\times S_{\Omega^c}$ (Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction}). We take the quotient of $S_\Omega\times S_{\Omega^c}$ by $S_{\Omega^c}$, the kernel of the action on $\Omega$ (Lemma \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance}). In this quotient, $C$ is hereditarily $S_d$-permutable. Moreover, the image $C$ of the action of $B$ on $\Omega$ is transitive by construction, and a transitive nonsolvable group has degree $d\geq5$.

The set $\{\langle e_i\rangle:i\in\Omega\}$ is permuted by $A$, so $A$ stabilizes the nondegenerate unitary coordinate subspace $V_\Omega=\langle e_i:i\in\Omega\rangle$. Let $J_\Omega$ be the stabilizer in $E$ of the orthogonal decomposition $V_\Omega\perp V_\Omega^\perp$. We restrict the hereditary condition of $A$ to $J_\Omega$. Let $K_\Omega$ be the complementary unitary factor of $J_\Omega$ on $V_\Omega^\perp$, acting on $V_\Omega^\perp$ and trivially on $V_\Omega$. To study the action on $V_\Omega$, we take the quotient $J_\Omega/K_\Omega$ and use its projective action $\rho_\Omega:J_\Omega/K_\Omega\to\operatorname{PGU}(V_\Omega)$ on $V_\Omega$. Write $E_\Omega=\rho_\Omega(J_\Omega/K_\Omega)$ and let $A_\Omega$ be the image of $A$ under $J_\Omega\to J_\Omega/K_\Omega\to E_\Omega$. Lemmas \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} and \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance} show that $A_\Omega$ is hereditarily $E_\Omega$-permutable, with $\operatorname{PSU}_d(Q)\leq E_\Omega\leq\operatorname{PGU}_d(Q)$. The permutation action of $A_\Omega$ on the simplex lines indexed by $\Omega$ has image $C$.

If $d\geq7$, then Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-transitive-alternating} shows that $C\geq A_d$ and Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-full-support-simplex} shows that the image of $A$ in $E_\Omega$ cannot have this permutation image $C$. If $d\in\{5,6\}$, then Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-small-simplex} shows that the image $A_\Omega$ of $A$ in $E_\Omega$ cannot have the nonsolvable permutation image $C$. Hence $B$ cannot be nonsolvable, so $B=1$. In every case $A\leq D$, and Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-toral} settles the case of a subgroup of the diagonal torus $D$ in $E$.

label: rmk:simplex-nonsolvable-reduction
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rmk:simplex-nonsolvable-reduction}
Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image} concerns the permutation image $B=AD/D$ of the unitary subgroup $A$ on the lines of a self-polar simplex. If $B$ has an orbit $\Omega$ of size $d=|\Omega|$ with nonsolvable image $C=B^\Omega$, then we restrict to the setwise stabilizer $S_\Omega\times S_{\Omega^c}$ of $\Omega$ and take its quotient by $S_{\Omega^c}$, the symmetric group on the complement of $\Omega$. This restriction and quotient make the image $C$ hereditarily permutable in the symmetric group on $\Omega$. Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-transitive-alternating} forces the transitive image $C$ to contain the alternating group, with the two actions of degree six treated in Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-small-simplex}. We then consider the image $A_\Omega$ of $A$ in $E_\Omega$ acting on the coordinate space $V_\Omega=\langle e_i:i\in\Omega\rangle$. These are the image group and coordinate space defined in the proof of Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image}. The indices of the parabolic stabilizers $P_1$ and $P_2$ of a totally singular line and a totally singular plane in $E_\Omega$ are divisible by a prime that does not divide the order of its simplex stabilizer $D_\Omega:S_d$, where $D_\Omega$ is the diagonal subgroup for the $d$ lines indexed by $\Omega$. If the unitary image of $A$ were contained in both parabolics, then we would have a $2$-dimensional submodule of the natural $A_d$-permutation module, contrary to Lemma \ref{lem:alternating-permutation-no-two}. Therefore, the permutation image of $A$ cannot contain the alternating group on the entire orbit.

label: thm:unitary-odd-prime-noncentral
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unitary-odd-prime-noncentral}
Let
$$
        G=\operatorname{PSU}_r(q),~ r\geq5\text{ odd prime},~ (r,q+1)=1,~ (r,q)\neq(5,2).
$$
Then every proper ordinary $G$-permutable subgroup $F<G$ has order $1$ or $r$, and $G$ has no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We use the self-polar simplex stabilizer $M=D:S_r$ in $G$, maximal by Dye \cite[Theorem 5]{Dye1985}. By Liebeck, Praeger and Saxl \cite[Corollary 2]{LPS1990}, a simple unitary group of odd dimension with a maximal factorization is one of $U_3(3)$, $U_3(5)$, $U_9(2)$. None has prime dimension $r\geq5$, so the product alternative $G=FM^x$ cannot occur. So Lemma \ref{lem:ordinary-maximal-product} shows that $F$ is contained in a $G$-conjugate of $M$, and every prime divisor of $|F|$ either divides $q+1$ or is at most $r$.

We let $T$ be a unitary Singer torus corresponding to a partition with one part. This torus lies in $G$ and has order $|T|=(q^r+1)/(q+1)$. By $G$-permutability of $F$, we have a subgroup $FT^x$ of $G$, and since $G$ has no factorization, $FT^x<G$. A maximal overgroup of $FT^x$ in $G$ contains $T^x$, so by Bereczky's theorem \cite[Main Theorem]{Bereczky2000}, that maximal overgroup lies in $N_G(T^x)$, whence
$$
        |F|\mid r\,\frac{q^r+1}{q+1}.
$$
If a prime $a\mid|F|$ divided $q+1$, then $a\mid r(q^r+1)/(q+1)$. Since $(q^r+1)/(q+1)\equiv r\pmod{q+1}$, the congruence forces $a=r$, contradicting $(r,q+1)=1$. So no prime divisor of $|F|$ divides $q+1$. If $a$ is an odd prime divisor of $|F|$, then $a\leq r$. If $a<r$, then $a\mid(q^r+1)/(q+1)$ with $a\nmid q+1$, so $-q$ has order $r$ modulo $a$ and $r\mid a-1$, impossible. Hence every odd prime divisor of $|F|$ is $r$, and $|F|\mid r$ as $r \nmid q^r +1$.

Now let $A$ be nontrivial and hereditarily $G$-permutable, so $|A|=r$. We choose a self-polar simplex stabilizer $D:S_r$ containing $A$. Since $r\nmid q+1$, the image of $A$ in $S_r$ has order $r$ and is generated by an $r$-cycle. Testing hereditary permutability of this image against the subgroup generated by a transposition in $S_r$, we have a subgroup of order $2r$. Therefore, the transposition normalizes the cyclic subgroup generated by the $r$-cycle. But
$$
        N_{S_r}(\langle (1\,2\,\cdots\,r)\rangle)=\operatorname{AGL}_1(r),
$$
whose nonidentity elements have at most one fixed point, while a transposition fixes $r-2\geq3$ points, a contradiction.

label: thm:unitary-psu52
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:unitary-psu52}
The group $G=\operatorname{PSU}_5(2)$ has no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $A<G$ be proper, nontrivial, and hereditarily $G$-permutable. The maximal subgroups of $G$ are listed in the \emph{Atlas of Finite Groups} \cite{Atlas1985}. By the result of Liebeck, Praeger, and Saxl \cite[Corollary 2]{LPS1990}, $G$ has no factorization. Indeed, their list of factorizable unitary groups of odd dimension omits $U_5(2)$. The group $G$ has a maximal subgroup
$$
        T\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(11).
$$
Since $G$ has no factorization $G=AT^x$, Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} shows that a $G$-conjugate of $A$ is contained in $T$. If $A<T$, then Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} and the result for $\operatorname{PSL}_2$ in Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-low-bases} contradict hereditary permutability of $A$, so $A=T$. Testing hereditary permutability of $T$ against the maximal subgroup $M\cong3^4:S_5$ of $G$, we have the subgroup $TM^x$ for a conjugate $M^x$ that permutes with $T$. Since $M^x$ is maximal, either $T\leq M^x$ or $G=TM^x$. Because $11\mid|T|$ but $11\nmid|M|$, $T$ cannot be contained in $M^x$, and the factorization $G=TM^x$ is impossible by \cite[Corollary 2]{LPS1990}. This contradiction proves the theorem.

label: lem:unitary-largest-prime
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-largest-prime}
Let $n$ be odd composite with $(n,q+1)=1$, and let $b=\max\pi(n)$, $u=n/b$. If $r\mid u$, then $r\nmid q^b+1$. Consequently, $(u,q^b+1)=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $r\mid u$, so $r\leq b$ and $r
mid q+1$. If $r<b$ and $r\mid q^b+1$, then $q^b\equiv-1$ and $q
ot\equiv-1\pmod r$. As $b$ is prime, $\operatorname{ord}_r(q)$ divides $2b$ but not $b$, and is not $2$, so $\operatorname{ord}_r(q)=2b$ and $2b\mid r-1$, impossible for $r<b$. If $r=b$, then $q^b\equiv q\pmod b$, so $q^b+1\equiv q+1
ot\equiv0\pmod b$. Hence $r
mid q^b+1$ in all cases.

label: prop:unitary-odd-noncentral-composite
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unitary-odd-noncentral-composite}
Let $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ with $n>3$ odd composite and $(n,q+1)=1$. Then $G$ has no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $A<G$ is proper, nontrivial, and hereditarily $G$-permutable. Let $b=\max\pi(n)$ and $u=n/b$. By \cite[\S4.3, Table 4.3.A]{KleidmanLiebeck1990}, the $\mathcal C_3$ normalizer of the subgroup defined over the extension field in $G$ is
$$
        E_b=N_G(S_b),~ S_b\cong\operatorname{PSU}_u(q^b).
$$ If hereditary $G$-permutability of $A$ and Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} for $E_b$ led to the product alternative $G = A E_b ^x$, then a maximal subgroup $M\geq A$ of $G$ would produce a maximal factorization $G=ME_b^x$. But neither the list of factorizations with maximal factors of $\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ nor its classical version has such a row under these hypotheses \cite[Main Theorem]{LPS1990}, \cite[Theorem 1.4, Tables 4.1--4.2]{LiWangXia2024}. So after conjugating $A$ in $G$, $A\leq E_b$.

If $A<S_b$, then $A$ is hereditarily $S_b$-permutable by Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction}, and by Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-largest-prime} $(u,q^b+1)=1$, so $S_b$ is again a unitary group of smaller odd dimension satisfying this coprimality condition. Induction on the dimension, with Theorems \ref{thm:unitary-low-bases}, \ref{thm:unitary-odd-prime-noncentral} and \ref{thm:unitary-psu52} as bases, settles the case of a proper subgroup of $S_b$.

We next show that $A=S_b$ is impossible. Under the assumption $A=S_b$, the subgroup $S_b$ itself is hereditarily $G$-permutable. Using Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} for a self-polar simplex stabilizer $\Delta=D:S_n$ in $G$, we then have $S_b\leq\Delta^x$ or $G=S_b\Delta^x$. By \cite[Corollary 2]{LPS1990}, the factorizable simple unitary groups of odd dimension are $U_3(3)$, $U_3(5)$ and $U_9(2)$. The groups $U_3(3)$ and $U_3(5)$ have dimension $3$, and $U_9(2)$ has $(9,q+1)>1$. None has $n$ odd composite with $(n,q+1)=1$. Therefore, the factorization $G=S_b\Delta^x$ is impossible under the present hypotheses. So $S_b\leq\Delta^x$. We relabel $\Delta^x$ as $\Delta$ and write $D$ for its diagonal subgroup. Using Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image} for the hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup $S_b$ of the stabilizer of a self-polar simplex, we have $S_bD/D=1$, i.e., $S_b\leq D$. Since $D$ is abelian while $S_b\cong\operatorname{PSU}_u(q^b)$ ($u\geq3$, $q^b\geq8$) is nonabelian simple, we cannot have $S_b\leq D$.

If $A\not\leq S_b$, then let $Q=AS_b/S_b\neq1$. We prove that $A$ is contained in a stabilizer of a self-polar simplex in $G$, independently of Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image}. The stabilizer $\Delta=D:S_n$ of a self-polar simplex is maximal in $G$ by Dye \cite[Theorem 5]{Dye1985}. We use hereditary $G$-permutability of $A$ and Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} for $\Delta$ with $A$ contained in $E_b$. Either $A\leq\Delta^x$ for some $x$, or $G=A\Delta^x$. In the latter case, a maximal subgroup $M\geq A$ produces a maximal factorization $G=M\Delta^x$ with the self-polar simplex stabilizer $\Delta^x$ as a factor. The only factorizable simple unitary groups of odd dimension are $U_3(3)$, $U_3(5)$, $U_9(2)$ \cite[Corollary 2]{LPS1990}. Since $n$ is odd composite, $n\neq3$. If $n=9$, then the condition $(9,q+1)=1$ is incompatible with $q\equiv2\pmod3$, so $q\neq2$. Hence $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ is none of the three listed factorizable groups. Therefore, the factorization $G=A\Delta^x$ is impossible. Hence $A\leq\Delta^x$. Relabelling $\Delta^x$ as $\Delta$ ($\Delta^x$ is again a self-polar simplex stabilizer, and $A$ was not moved), we have $A\leq E_b\cap\Delta$.

By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-extension-quotient},
$$
        \pi(Q)\subseteq\pi\!\left(b\,\frac{q^b+1}{q+1}\right),
$$
and since $b\nmid q+1$, Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-visibility-gcd} shows that the prime divisors of $|Q|$ are coprime to $q+1$. The permutation action $A\to B=AD/D$ on the lines of the self-polar simplex has kernel $A\cap D$. The order of this kernel has prime divisors only among those of $q+1$. Since $|Q|$ divides $|A|$ and every prime of $\pi(Q)$ is coprime to $q+1$, every prime of $\pi(Q)$ divides $|B|$. In particular $B\neq1$. But $A\leq E_b\cap\Delta$ is a hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup of the stabilizer of a self-polar simplex in the unitary descent, so by Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image} (see Remark \ref{rmk:simplex-nonsolvable-reduction}), we have $B=1$, a contradiction. Therefore, neither the case $A=S_b$ nor the case $A\not\leq S_b$ can occur.

label: lem:unitary-prime-pure-central
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-prime-pure-central}
Let $r\geq5$ be an odd prime with $r\mid q+1$. Then $G=\operatorname{PSU}_r(q)$ has no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $A<G$ be proper, nontrivial, and hereditarily $G$-permutable, and let $M=D:S_r$ be a self-polar simplex stabilizer, maximal in $G$ by Dye \cite[Theorem 5]{Dye1985}. If the product alternative $G = A M^x$ held with $M$, then $G$ would have a maximal factorization with a unitary socle of odd dimension. But the factorizable unitary groups of odd dimension are $U_3(3)$, $U_3(5)$, $U_9(2)$ \cite[Corollary 2]{LPS1990}. None has prime dimension $r\geq5$. So $A\leq M$ after conjugating $A$ in $G$. The image of $A$ in $M/D\cong S_r$ is handled by Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image} (see Remark \ref{rmk:simplex-nonsolvable-reduction}), and $AD/D = 1$ implies that $A\leq D$, which is impossible by Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-toral}.
head: environment

label: prop:unitary-odd-central
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unitary-odd-central}
Let $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$ with $n$ odd and $(n,q+1)>1$. Then $G$ has no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof into four steps.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 1.}] $A\leq\Delta$ after conjugation.
\end{itemize}
We begin with the prime dimensions that form the bases for induction. If $n=3$, then we use Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-low-bases}. If $n=r\geq5$ is prime, then $r\mid q+1$ and we use Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-prime-pure-central}. The rest of the proof concerns odd composite $n$. For a prime divisor $b$ of $n$, the descent below uses a subgroup $S_b\cong\operatorname{PSU}_{n/b}(q^b)$. If $A<S_b$, then we apply induction in $S_b$. This reduces the dimension from $n$ to $n/b$ and changes the field parameter from $q$ to $q^b$.

We need the permutation image of $A$ on the simplex lines in two cases. In one case, $A$ has nontrivial image in the quotient of the extension field normalizer by its socle. In the other, $A$ equals the socle of that normalizer. In both cases, we prove that the hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup $A$ is contained in a stabilizer $\Delta=D:S_n$ of a self-polar simplex in $G$, independently of Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image}. The stabilizer $\Delta$ is maximal in $G$ by Dye \cite[Theorem 5]{Dye1985}. Using Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} for $\Delta$, we have $A\leq\Delta^x$ unless $G=A\Delta^x$. In the latter case, a maximal subgroup $M\geq A$ of $G$ produces a maximal factorization $G=M\Delta^x$ with the self-polar simplex stabilizer $\Delta^x$ as a factor. By \cite[Corollary 2]{LPS1990}, the only factorizable simple unitary groups of odd dimension are $U_3(3),U_3(5),U_9(2)$. In the classical version, their factorizations have parabolic and almost simple factors, never a factor in class $\mathcal C_2$ that is a self-polar simplex stabilizer \cite[Theorem 1.4, Tables 4.1--4.2]{LiWangXia2024}. Therefore, no simple unitary group of odd dimension has such a factorization. Hence $A\leq\Delta^x$, and we relabel $\Delta^x$ as $\Delta$.

We consider the prime divisors of $n$ that do not divide $q+1$. Suppose that $n$ has a prime divisor not dividing $q+1$, and choose $b=\max(\pi(n)\setminus\pi(q+1))$. By \cite[\S4.3, Table 4.3.A]{KleidmanLiebeck1990}, the $\mathcal C_3$ normalizer of the subgroup defined over the extension field in $G$ is
$$
        E_b=N_G(S_b),~ S_b\cong\operatorname{PSU}_{n/b}(q^b).
$$

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 2.}] After descent, $\pi(n)\subseteq\pi(q+1)$.
\end{itemize}
As in Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-odd-noncentral-composite}, we distinguish the case where $A$ is contained in the socle $S_b$ from the case where the image of $A$ in the quotient of $E_b$ by $S_b$ is nontrivial. When the image of $A$ in this quotient is nontrivial, $b\nmid q+1$. In this case, we choose $\Delta$ to contain $A$ by the argument in Step~1 establishing that $A$ lies in a self-polar simplex stabilizer. The prime divisors of the image of $A$ in $E_b$ modulo $S_b$ then appear in the permutation image $B=AD/D$ of $A$ on the simplex lines (Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-visibility-gcd}). By Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image}, we have $B=1$, a contradiction (since the hypothesis $b\nmid q+1$ holds, we use Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-solvable-low-socle-simplex} when $B$ is solvable, see Remark \ref{rmk:simplex-nonsolvable-reduction}). We now suppose that $A\leq S_b$. If $A<S_b$, then the descent passes from dimension $n$ to dimension $n/b$, removing one factor $b$ from the dimension. Under the assumption $A<S_b$, take $r\mid n/b$ with $r\nmid q+1$. If $r=b$, then $q^b+1\equiv q+1\not\equiv0\pmod b$. If $r<b$ and $r\mid q^b+1$, then the order argument of Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-largest-prime} shows that $2b\mid r-1$, impossible. Every prime divisor of $n/b$ that does not divide $q^b+1$ is also a prime divisor of $n$ that does not divide $q+1$. Therefore, we use induction in $S_b$. Repeating this descent reduces to the case $\pi(n)\subseteq\pi(q+1)$. If $A=S_b$, then $S_b$ is hereditarily $G$-permutable. The factorization argument in Step~1 makes the product $G=S_b\Delta^x$ impossible. Therefore, we choose a stabilizer $\Delta$ of a self-polar simplex containing $S_b$ by Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product}. We use Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image} to conclude that $S_bD/D=1$, so $S_b\leq D$. Since $D$ is abelian while $S_b\cong\operatorname{PSU}_{n/b}(q^b)$ ($n/b\geq3$, $q^b\geq8$) is nonabelian simple, we cannot have $S_b\leq D$.

Now assume that $\pi(n)\subseteq\pi(q+1)$. Since the cases of prime dimension have been settled, suppose that $n$ is composite. We choose the largest prime $b=\max\pi(n)$ and let $u=n/b\geq3$. By \cite[\S4.3, Table 4.3.A]{KleidmanLiebeck1990}, the $\mathcal C_3$ normalizer of the subgroup defined over the extension field is
$$
        E_b=N_G(S_b),~ S_b\cong\operatorname{PSU}_u(q^b).
$$

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 3.}] $A\leq E_b$ and $A\not\leq S_b$.
\end{itemize}
By Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product}, after conjugating $A$ in $G$, either $A\leq E_b$ or $G=AE_b^x$. In the product case a maximal subgroup $M\geq A$ of $G$ produces a maximal factorization $G=ME_b^x$ with the subgroup $E_b^x$ as a factor in class $\mathcal C_3$ that fixes an extension field structure as a whole. By \cite[Corollary 2]{LPS1990}, the only factorizable simple unitary groups of odd dimension are $U_3(3)$, $U_3(5)$ and $U_9(2)$, and only $U_9(2)$ meets the present hypotheses ($n=9$, $q=2$, $b=3$, $S_b\cong\operatorname{PSU}_3(8)$). The only factorization of $U_9(2)$ with a nonsolvable factor is $U_9(2)=J_3\cdot P_1$, where $P_1=2^{1+14}{:}\operatorname{SU}_7(2)$ is the parabolic subgroup stabilizing a singular line in the natural module of $U_9(2)$ \cite[Lemma 5.7]{LiWangXia2024}. Since $E_b^x$ is nonsolvable (the group $E_b^x$ contains $\operatorname{PSU}_3(8)$) but is a $\mathcal C_3$ subgroup defined over an extension field, hence neither the almost simple factor $J_3$ nor the parabolic $P_1$, no such factorization exists. Hence, after conjugating $A$ in $G$, $A\leq E_b$.

If $A<S_b$, then $A$ is hereditarily $S_b$-permutable (Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction}). Since $b$ is odd and $b\mid q+1$, every prime $r\mid q+1$ has $q^b\equiv-1\pmod r$. Therefore, $\pi(u)\subseteq\pi(n)\subseteq\pi(q+1)\subseteq\pi(q^b+1)$. The group $S_b\cong\operatorname{PSU}_u(q^b)$ is again a unitary group of odd dimension with every prime divisor of $u$ dividing $q^b+1$, in the smaller dimension $u<n$. Induction on the dimension, with the bases of Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-low-bases} and Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-prime-pure-central}, settles the case of a proper subgroup of $S_b$.

We next show that $A=S_b$ is impossible. Under the assumption $A=S_b$, the subgroup $S_b$ is hereditarily $G$-permutable. By Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} for a self-polar simplex stabilizer $\Delta=D:S_n$ in $G$, we then have $S_b\leq\Delta^x$ or $G=S_b\Delta^x$. By the factorization list for the extension field normalizer $E_b=N_G(S_b)$ used in Step~3 (for $U_9(2)$ the only factorization is $J_3\cdot P_1$, with no self-polar simplex stabilizer as a factor), the factorization $G=S_b\Delta^x$ is impossible. So $S_b\leq\Delta^x$. We relabel $\Delta^x$ as $\Delta$ and write $D$ for its diagonal subgroup. Using Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image} for the hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup $S_b$ of the stabilizer of a self-polar simplex, we have $S_bD/D=1$, i.e., $S_b\leq D$. Since $D$ is abelian while $S_b\cong\operatorname{PSU}_u(q^b)$ ($u\geq3$, $q^b\geq8$) is nonabelian simple, we cannot have $S_b\leq D$.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 4.}] $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
If $A\not\leq S_b$, then let $Q=AS_b/S_b\neq1$. By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-extension-quotient},
$$
        \pi(Q)\subseteq\pi\!\left(b\,\frac{q^b+1}{q+1}\right),
$$
and since
$$
        \frac{q^b+1}{q+1}=q^{b-1}-q^{b-2}+\cdots-q+1\equiv b\pmod{q+1},
$$
a prime of $\pi(Q)$ dividing the diagonal $(q+1)$-part of the simplex stabilizer can only be $b$. We next prove that $A$ is contained in a conjugate of a stabilizer $\Delta=D:S_n$ of a self-polar simplex in $G$. As $A\leq E_b$, a product $G=A\Delta^x$ would produce a maximal factorization $G=M'\Delta^x$ (with $M'\geq A$ maximal in $G$) having a self-polar simplex stabilizer as a factor. The factorization $G=M'\Delta^x$ is forbidden by the list for the extension field normalizer $E_b$ used in Step~3. Therefore, $A\leq\Delta^x$. Relabelling $\Delta^x$ as $\Delta$ and writing $D$ for its diagonal subgroup, we have $A\leq E_b\cap\Delta$. Let $B=AD/D$ be the image of $A$ in its permutation action on the simplex lines. The kernel of the permutation action from $A$ to $B$ on the simplex lines is $A\cap D$. The order of this kernel has prime divisors only among those of $q+1$. Therefore, every prime of $\pi(Q)$ coprime to $q+1$ divides $|B|$. A prime $r\mid(q^b+1)/(q+1)$ with $r\nmid q+1$ has $\operatorname{ord}_r(q)=2b$, hence $r\geq2b+1\geq7$, and by Lemma \ref{lem:solvable-simplex-prime-bound} divides the order of no solvable hereditarily $S_n$-permutable permutation image of $A$ on the simplex lines. If the prime $r$ divided the order of $B$, then $B$ would be nonsolvable, contradicting Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image}. So no such prime occurs. By Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-simplex-image}, we have $B=1$ in any case. Then $A\leq D$ is diagonal and Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-toral} forces $A=1$, against assumption. Therefore, $A\leq S_b$, and repeating the descent through proper subgroups of $S_b$ reduces to the bases of prime dimension $r$ with $r\mid q+1$, the base in dimension three in Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-low-bases} and the higher prime bases in Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-prime-pure-central}.

label: lem:unitary-flag-toral
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:unitary-flag-toral}
Let $G=\operatorname{PSU}_{2m}(q)$ and let $A$ be a hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup lying in a parabolic subgroup $P$ of $G$. Suppose that the image $C$ of $A$ in the Levi quotient $P/R_u(P)$ lies in the central torus of this Levi quotient. In this situation, the image of $A$ in each semisimple factor of this Levi quotient is trivial. Then $C=1$, so $A\leq R_u(P)$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The image of $A$ in each semisimple factor of the Levi quotient of $P$ is trivial. Therefore, the subgroup $A$ lies in a Borel subgroup $B$ of $G=\operatorname{PSU}_{2m}(q)$ with maximal torus $T$ in $B$. Identify $B/R_u(B)$ with the maximal torus $T$. We use $C$ for the image of $A$ under $B\to B/R_u(B)\cong T$. The characters of $T$ are spanned by the simple roots $\alpha_1,\dots,\alpha_m$ relative to $B$, so it suffices to prove $\alpha_i(C)=1$ for every $i$. Then $C$ lies in the intersection of the kernels of the simple root characters, namely the scalar centre before taking the projective quotient, and is projectively scalar, i.e., $C=1$.

We fix $i$ and let $P_i\geq B$ be the minimal parabolic of $G$ corresponding to the simple root indexed by $i$, with Levi decomposition $P_i=L_iR_u(P_i)$. By \cite[Proposition 26.1(b)]{MalleTesterman2011} and \cite{Carter1985}, the semisimple factor of rank one of $L_i$ is $\operatorname{SL}_2(q')$ with $q'=q^2$ on a linear simple root and $q'=q$ on the unitary simple root. Since $A\leq B\leq P_i$, Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} makes $A$ hereditarily $P_i$-permutable. Since $R_u(P_i)\unlhd P_i$, Lemma \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance} makes the image of $A$ in $L_i\cong P_i/R_u(P_i)$ hereditarily $L_i$-permutable. The relevant action is that of $L_i$ on the factor of rank one. We take the quotient of $L_i$ by the product of its central torus and the kernel of this action. This product is a normal subgroup of $L_i$, so Lemma \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance} applies again. It follows that the image $\bar A_i$ of $A$ is hereditarily $E_i$-permutable in the quotient group $E_i$, with $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q')\leq E_i\leq\operatorname{PGL}_2(q')$. Since $A\leq B$, the image $\bar A_i$ lies in the image of $B$ in $E_i$, a Borel subgroup (point stabilizer) of $E_i$, and the diagonal part of $\bar A_i$ is exactly $\alpha_i(C)$. When $q'\geq3$, by Lemma \ref{lem:pgl2-borel}, we have $\bar A_i=1$, so $\alpha_i(C)=1$. The only remaining value is $q'=2$ (the unitary simple root with $q=2$), where the diagonal torus of $\operatorname{PGL}_2(2)$ is trivial, so $\alpha_i(C)=1$ also in this case. Hence $\alpha_i(C)=1$ for every $i$, so $C=1$. The image of $A$ in the Levi quotient $P/R_u(P)$ is trivial, so $A\leq R_u(P)$.

title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:unitary-even}
For the simple group $G=\operatorname{PSU}_{2m}(q)$ there is no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For ease of reading, we divide the proof into seven steps. For $m=1$, the isomorphism $\operatorname{PSU}_2(q)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ reduces the required nonexistence of proper nontrivial hereditarily permutable subgroups to Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-low-bases}. Therefore, we may assume that $m\geq2$, and let $A<G$ be proper, nontrivial, and hereditarily $G$-permutable.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 1.}] If $G=AN_1$, then $G=AP_1^y$.
\end{itemize}
Let $N_1$ be the stabilizer in $G$ of a nondegenerate line of the natural unitary space $V$, a maximal $\mathcal C_1$-subgroup of type $\operatorname{GU}_1(q)\perp\operatorname{GU}_{2m-1}(q)$ \cite[Table 3.5.B]{KleidmanLiebeck1990}. By hereditary $G$-permutability of $A$ and Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product}, after conjugating $A$ in $G$ either $A\leq N_1$ or $G=AN_1$. Suppose that $G=AN_1$, and take a maximal subgroup $M\geq A$ of $G$, so $G=MN_1$ is a maximal factorization. We use the reduction to factorizations with maximal factors of Liebeck, Praeger, and Saxl \cite[Main Theorem, Corollary 1]{LPS1990}. The possible unitary factorizations with $N_1$ as a factor are in Li, Wang, and Xia \cite[Theorem 4.1, Tables 4.1--4.2, Proposition 4.2]{LiWangXia2024}. The solvable case is covered by Li and Xia \cite{LiXia2022}.

We show directly that the factorization $G=AN_1$ is impossible. Let $P_1$ be a stabilizer of a singular line in $G$. The subgroup $N_1$ has at least two orbits on singular lines of $V$ (those in the orthogonal complement of the nondegenerate line fixed by $N_1$, and those outside that orthogonal complement), so $P_1^gN_1\neq G$ for all $g\in G$. Hence, if $A\leq P_1^g$, then the assumed product case $G=AN_1$ would force $G\leq P_1^gN_1<G$, a contradiction, so $A$ lies in no $G$-conjugate of $P_1$. By hereditary permutability of $A$ with $P_1$ and maximality of $P_1$ in $G$, we then have the factorization
\begin{equation}\label{eq:even-p1-index}
        G=AP_1^y,~\text{so}~ |G:P_1|\mid|A|.
\end{equation}
Using the unitary order formulas \cite[Propositions 2.3.1--2.3.3]{KleidmanLiebeck1990}, we obtain
$$
        |G:P_1|=\frac{(q^{2m}-1)(q^{2m-1}+1)}{q^2-1}.
$$
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 2.}] $A\leq N_1$ after conjugation.
\end{itemize}
For $e=4m-2$, Zsigmondy \cite{Zsigmondy1892} gives a primitive prime divisor $r$ of $q^e-1$, except when $(q,e)=(2,6)$. The prime $r$ divides $q^{2m-1}+1$, divides $|G:P_1|$, and divides neither $q^{2m}-1$ nor the extension-degree parts of the Singer and parabolic rows. So the solvable $P_m$/Singer row and the generic nonsolvable $N_1$-rows cannot satisfy \eqref{eq:even-p1-index}. Writing $G=MN_1$ for a maximal subgroup $M\geq A$ of $G$, the relation \eqref{eq:even-p1-index} forces $r\mid|A|$, hence $r\mid|M|$. But no maximal subgroup of $G$ serving as the factor paired with $N_1$ in \cite[Theorem 4.1, Tables 4.1--4.2]{LiWangXia2024} has order divisible by this primitive prime divisor $r$ of $q^{4m-2}-1$.

The primitive prime divisor argument leaves the small cases $\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$ and the $\operatorname{PSU}_6(2)$ row with factor $3\cdot M_{22}$ \cite[Table 4.1, Proposition 4.2]{LiWangXia2024}. For $\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$, the ATLAS \cite{Atlas1985} gives
$$
        |G|=25920,~ |G:N_1|=40,~ |G:P_1|=45,~ |G:P_2|=27,
$$
with $|N_1|,|P_1|,|P_2|=648,576,960$. The factorization $G = AN_1$ bounds the order of $A$ by the order of the factor $S_6$, so $|A|\mid720$, while the factorization $G = AN_1$ also shows that $40\mid|A|$. Testing the hereditary permutability of $A$ with $P_1$, we have $45\mid|A|$, hence $360\mid|A|$. Then no $G$-conjugate of $P_2$ (order $960=2^6\cdot3\cdot5$) contains $A$, and testing the  hereditary permutability of $A$ with $P_2$ forces $27\mid|A|$, contradicting $|A|\mid720=2^4\cdot3^2\cdot5$. For the $\operatorname{PSU}_6(2)$ row,
$$
        |G:N_1|=672,~ |G:P_2|=6237=3^4\cdot7\cdot11,~ |P_2|=2^{15}\cdot3^2\cdot5,
$$
and $|3\cdot M_{22}|=2^7\cdot3^3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11$, so the factorization with $N_1$ shows that $7\mid|A|$, $A$ is in no $G$-conjugate of $P_2$, and the factorization with $P_2$ forces $3^4\mid|A|$, again a contradiction. Hence $G=AN_1$ is impossible, and after conjugating $A$ in $G$, $A\leq N_1$.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 3.}] $A$ fixes a singular line.
\end{itemize}
We test $A\leq N_1$ against a singular line stabilizer $P_1$ in $G$. If $A$ lay in no conjugate of $P_1$, then hereditary permutability of $A$ and maximality of $P_1$ would force $G=AP_1^y$ and $|G:P_1|\mid|A|\mid|N_1|$. The subgroup $N_1$ has type $\operatorname{GU}_1(q)\times\operatorname{GU}_{2m-1}(q)$, whose primes other than the characteristic lie among $q+1$ and $q^i-(-1)^i$ for $1\leq i\leq2m-1$ \cite[Propositions 2.3.1--2.3.3]{KleidmanLiebeck1990}. Zsigmondy's theorem \cite{Zsigmondy1892} guarantees the primitive prime divisors in the following two cases. For $m$ even, a primitive prime divisor of $q^{2m}-1$ divides the $q^{2m}-1$ factor of $|G:P_1|$ and no factor of $|N_1|$. For $m$ odd, since the only factor of $|N_1|$ with exponent divisible by $m$ is $q^m+1$, a primitive prime divisor of $q^m-1$ divides $|G:P_1|$ but not $|N_1|$. The only exception is $\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$. By the ATLAS \cite{Atlas1985}, $|G:P_1|=45\nmid648=|N_1|$. Thus, $|G:P_1|\nmid|N_1|$. So $A\leq P_1^y$. (For $\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$, one more test with $P_2$ shows that $|G:P_2|=27\nmid576=|P_1|$, so $A\leq P_2^z$.) If the singular line $\ell$ and totally singular plane $X$ stabilized by $A$ in $V$ satisfy $\ell\not\leq X$, then consider $X\cap\ell^\perp$. Since $\ell^\perp$ is a hyperplane, the intersection $X\cap\ell^\perp$ is nonzero. If $X\cap\ell^\perp$ were all of $X$, then $X\leq\ell^\perp$, hence $\ell\leq X^\perp=X$ (as $X^\perp=X$ for the maximal totally singular plane $X$). This would contradict $\ell\not\leq X$. So $X\cap\ell^\perp$ has dimension one and is an $A$-stable singular line $\ell'\leq X$. Replacing $\ell$ by $\ell'$, we have the flag $\ell'<X$, and $A$ lies in the parabolic subgroup $P_{\ell'<X}$ of $G$ stabilizing the singular flag $\ell'<X$. This parabolic has a toral Levi quotient and unipotent radical $R_u(P_{\ell'<X})$. The image of $A$ in the toral Levi quotient $P_{\ell'<X}/R_u(P_{\ell'<X})$ is trivial by Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-flag-toral}. For $\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$, the proof of Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-flag-toral} uses the subgroup $\operatorname{SL}_2(4)$ corresponding to the linear simple root as its factor of rank one, and $\operatorname{PSL}_2(4)\cong A_5$ is covered by Lemma \ref{lem:pgl2-borel}. The triviality of this toral image means that $A$ is contained in the unipotent radical $R_u(P_{\ell'<X})$ of $P_{\ell'<X}$. We now use the argument in Step 6 involving fixed spaces for $A$ in a unipotent radical. This argument shows that $A$ is the subgroup $\langle t\rangle$ generated by a single transvection. Such a subgroup cannot be hereditarily permutable by Appendix \ref{app:psu4-2}.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 4.}] If $\ell\not\leq U^\perp$, then $A\leq P_m^x$.
\end{itemize}
Now $A$ stabilizes a nondegenerate line $U$ and a singular line $\ell$ in the natural unitary space $V$. The group $\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$ was handled using its parabolic subgroup stabilizing the singular flag in Step 3, so assume that $(q,m)\neq(2,2)$. The stabilizers of the nondegenerate line $U$ and the singular line $\ell$ are geometric maximal subgroups of $G$ \cite[Table 3.5.B]{KleidmanLiebeck1990}.

Suppose that $\ell\not\leq U^\perp$. Then $H=U+\ell$ is a nondegenerate plane and $A$ lies in the stabilizer $N_2$ of $H$ in $G$. We have $V=H\perp W$ with nondegenerate orthogonal complement $W$ and $\dim W=2m-2$. We next prove that $A$ is contained in a parabolic subgroup of $G$ stabilizing a maximal totally singular subspace of $V$. With $P_m$ the stabilizer in $G$ of a maximal totally singular $m$-space of $V$, if $A$ lay in no $G$-conjugate of $P_m$, then by Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product}, we would have
$$
        G=AP_m^x,~ |G:P_m|\mid|A|\mid|N_2|.
$$
By the unitary order formula \cite[Propositions 2.3.1--2.3.3]{KleidmanLiebeck1990},
$$
        |G:P_m|=\prod_{i=1}^m(q^{2i-1}+1),
$$
while the factors in the part of $|N_2|$ prime to $p$ (with $N_2$ of type $\operatorname{GU}_2(q)\times\operatorname{GU}_{2m-2}(q)$) have exponents at most $2m-2$ apart from the factor on the nondegenerate plane $H$. Zsigmondy's theorem \cite{Zsigmondy1892} guarantees a primitive prime divisor of $q^{4m-2}-1$, except for the group $\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$ with $(q,4m-2)=(2,6)$. We settled this case in Step 3. The primitive prime divisor divides the last factor $q^{2m-1}+1$ of $|G:P_m|$. The multiplicative order of $q$ modulo this prime is $4m-2$, so the prime does not divide $|N_2|$. So $|G:P_m|\nmid|N_2|$, and $A\leq P_m^x$.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 5.}] The semisimple Levi factors are linear or of rank one.
\end{itemize}
We let $Y=X\cap W$ for the totally singular $m$-space $X$ stabilized by $P_m^x$ and by $A$. In $Y^\perp/Y$, the orthogonal complement $Y^\perp$ is taken inside $W$. Since $X$ is totally singular of dimension $m$ and $W$ has Witt index $m-1$, the projection of $X$ to $H$ is nonzero of dimension at most $2$, so
$$
        \dim Y=m-1\text{ or }m-2,~ \dim(Y^\perp/Y)=0\text{ or }2.
$$
The parabolic subgroup stabilizing $Y$ in the unitary group on $W$ has Levi factors $\operatorname{GL}(Y)$ and $\operatorname{GU}(Y^\perp/Y)$, and toral factors, together with the unipotent radical of this parabolic subgroup \cite[Proposition 26.1(b)]{MalleTesterman2011}. When $\ell\not\leq U^\perp$ and $H$ is nondegenerate, we need only consider a linear factor over $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$, toral factors, a case involving a unipotent radical, and possibly a quotient of rank one $\operatorname{PSU}_2(q)\leq E\leq\operatorname{PGU}_2(q)\cong\operatorname{PGL}_2(q)$ \cite[p. 66]{Wilson2009}.

Instead suppose that $\ell\leq U^\perp$, and let $W=U^\perp$, of odd dimension $2m-1$ and Witt index $m-1$, with $A$ stabilizing $U$ and the singular line $\ell\leq W$. Testing hereditary permutability of $A$ in $G$ against $P_m$ as in the case $\ell\not\leq U^\perp$, where $H=U+\ell$ is nondegenerate, we find that $A$ now lies in a subgroup $N_3$ of $G$ that stabilizes both $U$ and $\ell$, with Levi factors of types $\operatorname{GU}_1(q)$, $\operatorname{GL}_1(q^2)$, $\operatorname{GU}_{2m-3}(q)$. The parts of their orders prime to $p$ have no prime divisor for which $q$ has multiplicative order $4m-2$, whereas $|G:P_m|$ has such a prime divisor \cite{Zsigmondy1892}, so $|G: P_m| \nmid |N_3|$ and $A\leq P_m^x$. The totally singular $m$-space $X$ stabilized by $P_m^x$ and by $A$ has intersection $Y=X\cap W$ with $W$. Since $W$ has codimension $1$, the intersection $Y$ has dimension at least $m-1$. On the other hand, the Witt index of $W$ is $m-1$, so the dimension of $Y$ is not $m$. Together with the lower bound, this shows that the intersection $Y=X\cap W$ has dimension $m-1$. Therefore, the Levi quotient of the stabilizer of $Y$ in the unitary group on $W$ is linear of type $\operatorname{GL}_{m-1}(q^2)$. The other parts of this parabolic subgroup are toral factors and its unipotent radical.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 6.}] If $m\geq3$ and $A\leq R_u(P_m)$, then $A$ fixes $H$ pointwise.
\end{itemize}
An image of $A$ on $W$ lying in no subspace stabilizer in $\operatorname{PSU}(W)$ would, by hereditary permutability with a Borel subgroup of $\operatorname{PSU} (W)$, produce a factorization of  $\operatorname{PSU} (W)$ with a solvable factor that is a Borel subgroup. Since the $p$-part of this Borel subgroup is too large, this factorization is impossible by Li and Xia \cite{LiXia2022}. Hence the image of $A$ on $W$ lies in a parabolic subgroup of $\operatorname{PSU} (W)$. The argument forcing the image of $A$ to stabilize a line and a hyperplane reduces the linear rank. For the remaining cases of small rank in which the image contains the socle, we reduce to $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q^2)$, toral, or unipotent cases by Section \ref{sec:split-linear}. The linear images are handled by Theorem \ref{thm:split-linear}. The quotient of rank one $E$ from the projective action on $Y^\perp/Y$, when $\dim(Y^\perp/Y)=2$, is handled as follows. If $q>2$, then $E\not\cong\operatorname{PGL}_2(2)$ and Lemma \ref{lem:pgl2-borel} settles the image of $A$ in $E$. If $q=2$, then $E\cong\operatorname{PGL}_2(2)\cong S_3$. An image of $A$ in a point stabilizer of $E$ fixes a line in the natural $\mathbb{F}_2$-module for $E$. To extend the singular flag stabilized by $A$, we lift this invariant line in the natural $\mathbb{F}_2$-module for $E$, leaving only toral or unipotent images. By contrast, an image of $A$ in $E$ containing a subgroup of order $3$ has no invariant line on the natural $\mathbb{F}_2$-module for $E$. The lemma on invariant lines in modules, Lemma \ref{lem:sl-root-line-module-obstruction}, contradicts hereditary permutability of this image of $A$.

We now consider the case in which $A$ lies in a unipotent radical. $A\leq R_u(P_m)$ fixes the totally singular $m$-space $X$ pointwise. Moreover $A$ acts on the nondegenerate line $U$ through $\operatorname{GU}_1(q)$, cyclic of order $q+1$ and so a $p'$-group, so the $p$-group $A$ fixes $U$ pointwise as well. Hence every nonidentity $a\in A$ has $\operatorname{Fix}(a)\supseteq X\oplus U$, of dimension $m+1$. If $m=2$, then the fixed space of $a$ is a hyperplane of $V$, so $a$ is an element corresponding to a long root and $A$ lies in a single subgroup corresponding to a long root $T_v$ of $G$. By Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-unipotent-root-sl2}, we have $A=1$ for $q\geq3$, while $\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$ is settled by Appendix \ref{app:psu4-2}. If $m\geq3$, then recall that $A\leq R_u(P_m)$ fixes the maximal totally singular subspace $X$ of $V$ pointwise. Since $U$ is nondegenerate, $X\not\leq U^\perp$. Otherwise $U\leq X^\perp=X$, impossible for a nondegenerate line lying in a totally singular space. Therefore, we may choose a singular line $\ell'\leq X$ with $\ell'\not\leq U^\perp$. We pick nonzero vectors $u\in U$ and $w'\in\ell'$. We use the field norm $N(z)=z^{q+1}$ from $\mathbb{F}_{q^2}$ to $\mathbb{F}_q$. As $\langle w',w'\rangle=0$ and $\langle u,w'\rangle\neq0$, the Hermitian form on $H=\langle u,w'\rangle$ has Gram determinant $\langle u,u\rangle\langle w',w'\rangle-\langle u,w'\rangle\langle w',u\rangle=-N(\langle u,w'\rangle)\neq0$. Thus, $H=U+\ell'$ is a nondegenerate plane. By the argument at the start of this paragraph, $A$ fixes $U$ pointwise, and $A$ fixes $\ell'\leq X$ pointwise, so $A$ fixes $H=U+\ell'$ pointwise. Therefore, $A$ fixes the nondegenerate line $H\cap U^\perp=U^{\perp_H}$ pointwise.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=0pt,labelwidth=4em,labelsep=0.5em,itemindent=4.5em,align=left,topsep=3pt,partopsep=0pt,parsep=0pt,itemsep=0pt]
\item[{\bf Step 7.}] $A=1$.
\end{itemize}
Since $A$ fixes $U$ pointwise, the group $A$ lies in its stabilizer. In the matrix unitary group on $V$, the stabilizer of $U$ has the description $\operatorname{Stab}(U)=\operatorname{GU}_1(U)\times\operatorname{GU}(U^\perp)$. We restrict hereditary permutability of $A$ to this stabilizer. To obtain the action of this stabilizer on $U^\perp$, we then take the quotient of this stabilizer by the $\operatorname{GU}_1(U)$-factor of ${\rm Stab} (U)$, which is the kernel of that action (Lemmas \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} and \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance}). Therefore, the image of $A$ in $\operatorname{GU}(U^\perp)\cong\operatorname{GU}_{2m-1}(q)$ is a hereditarily $\operatorname{GU}_{2m-1}(q)$-permutable $p$-subgroup fixing the nondegenerate line $H\cap U^\perp=U^{\perp_H}$ in $U^\perp$. We take the quotient of $\operatorname{GU}_{2m-1}(q)$ by its centre to form the projective group $\operatorname{PGU}_{2m-1}(q) $. Since $\operatorname{PGU}_{2m-1}(q)/\operatorname{PSU}_{2m-1}(q)$ has order dividing $q+1$, a $p'$-number, the image of the $p$-subgroup coming from $A$ under the central quotient of the unitary group on $U^\perp$ lies in the simple socle $\operatorname{PSU}_{2m-1}(q)$. By Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} the projective image of $A$ is hereditarily $\operatorname{PSU}_{2m-1}(q)$-permutable. Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-unipotent} (odd dimension $2m-1\geq5$) makes the image of $A$ in $\operatorname{PSU}_{2m-1} (q)$ trivial. As $A$ fixes $U$, $A=1$.

We are left with linear images of $A$, images of rank one, images in a torus, or images in a unipotent radical. For the linear images we use Theorem \ref{thm:split-linear}, and for the images of rank one we use Lemma \ref{lem:pgl2-borel}, together with the argument for $q=2$ in the quotient of rank one. Let $\mathcal F$ be the singular flag stabilized by $A$ at a step of the descent, and let $P_{\mathcal F}=\operatorname{Stab}_G(\mathcal F)$ be its parabolic stabilizer, containing $A$. The toral image $C=AR_u(P_{\mathcal F})/R_u(P_{\mathcal F})$ lies in the central torus of the Levi quotient $P_{\mathcal F}/R_u(P_{\mathcal F})$. Hence Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-flag-toral} shows that this Levi image $C$ is trivial. Therefore, $A$ is contained in the unipotent radical $R_u(P_{\mathcal F})$ of $P_{\mathcal F}$. We then use the argument in Steps 6 and 7 with the fixed spaces of the elements of $A$ and the nondegenerate line $U$ to conclude that $A$ is trivial. This completes the proof in even dimension.

body_md: For $G=\operatorname{PSU}_n(q)$, the cases $n=2,3$ are the known cases for $\operatorname{PSL}_2$ and $\operatorname{PSU}_3$. If $n$ is an odd prime with $(n,q+1)=1$, then use Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-odd-prime-noncentral}, with the case $\operatorname{PSU}_5(2)$ from Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-psu52}. If $n$ is an odd prime with $n\mid q+1$, then use Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-prime-pure-central}. If $n$ is odd composite with $(n,q+1)=1$, then use Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-odd-noncentral-composite}. If $n$ is odd composite with $(n,q+1)>1$, then use Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-odd-central}. If $n$ is even, then use Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-even}. These cases cover all simple unitary groups.

title: Remark
body_md: The descent in Proposition \ref{prop:unitary-odd-noncentral-composite} uses the largest prime divisor $b=\max\pi(n)$ of the dimension (Lemma \ref{lem:unitary-largest-prime}). The lemma ensures that the dimension $u$ of the smaller unitary group is coprime to $q^b+1$, where $q^b$ is the unitary field parameter in $S_b\cong\operatorname{PSU}_u(q^b)$. By contrast, a smaller prime divisor of the dimension need not have this coprimality property.

body_md:
\label{prop:symplectic-no-p1-factorization}
For a simple group $G=\operatorname{PSp}_{2m}(q)$ with $(m,q)\neq(2,3)$, the case $G=AP_1^x$ cannot occur for a proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup $A$. The group $\operatorname{PSp}_4(3)$ is handled through $\operatorname{PSp}_4(3)\cong\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$ and {\rm Theorem \ref{thm:unitary}}.

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $G=AP_1^x$, so $A$ is transitive on isotropic lines. For $A$, we consider a parabolic of $G$ stabilizing a nonzero totally isotropic subspace $W$. This parabolic maps the nonempty proper set of isotropic lines in $W$ to itself, so this parabolic subgroup cannot contain $A$. We test hereditary $G$-permutability of $A$ with a Borel subgroup $B$ of $G$. Therefore, for some $G$-conjugate $B^y$, the product $AB^y$ is a subgroup. If $AB^y<G$, then a maximal subgroup of $G$ containing $AB^y$ contains the Borel subgroup $B^y$ and is parabolic, contradicting the fact that $A$ lies in no proper parabolic subgroup of $G$. Consequently, $G=AB^y$. In particular, for a maximal subgroup $M\geq A$ of $G$, we get the factorization $G=MB^y$ with solvable factor $B^y$. This factorization is covered by the classification of Li and Xia \cite{LiXia2022}.

A Borel subgroup of $G$, of type $C_m$, has $|B|_p=q^{m^2}$. For a symplectic socle $G$, the Li and Xia cases used for the factorization $G=MB^y$ are Table 1.1, rows 3--5, and Table 1.2, rows 12--17. The $\operatorname{PSp}_4(3)$ rows are omitted and handled through $\operatorname{PSp}_4(3)\cong\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$ and Theorem \ref{thm:unitary}. The comparison is as follows.
$$
\begin{array}{c|c|c|c}
\text{row} & \text{socle }G & \text{solvable }p\text{-part} & \text{Borel }p\text{-part}\\\hline
\text{1.1, row 3} & \operatorname{PSp}_{2m}(q),\ q\text{ even} & q^{m(m+1)/2} & q^{m^2}\\
\text{1.1, rows 4--5} & \operatorname{PSp}_4(q) & q^3 & q^4\\
\text{1.2, rows 12--15} & \operatorname{PSp}_4(q),\ q=5,7,11,23 & q^3 & q^4\\
\text{1.2, row 16} & \operatorname{Sp}_6(2) & \leq 2^4 & 2^9\\
\text{1.2, row 17} & \operatorname{PSp}_6(3) & 3^5 & 3^9
\end{array}
$$
In every row of this table, the $p$-part of the listed solvable factor is smaller than the $p$-part of a Borel subgroup of its symplectic socle $G$. Hence $B^y$ is not a listed factor, contradicting $G=MB^y$.

label: lem:symplectic-actual-levi-alternatives
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:symplectic-actual-levi-alternatives}
At a step of the symplectic descent, consider the singular line stabilizer used at that step and its projective Levi quotient. Let $S=\operatorname{PSp}_{2d}(q)\leq E\leq\operatorname{PCSp}_{2d}(q)$ be the symplectic factor of this quotient, with $d\geq2$ and $(d,q)\neq(2,2)$. Let $C\leq E$ be hereditarily $E$-permutable. Suppose that the image of $C$ in the semisimple factor of this quotient is nontrivial and does not contain the socle $S$. Then $C$ lies in the normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic of $S$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $B_S$ be a Borel subgroup of $S$ and $B_E=N_E(B_S)$, so the image of $B_E$ under the quotient map from $E$ to $E/S$ is the whole quotient. Suppose that $C$ lies in no normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic of $S$. By hereditary $E$-permutability of $C$, we have $B_E^x$ for some $x \in E$ with $CB_E^x$ a subgroup of $E$. Suppose that $CB_E^x<E$. Since $B_E^x$ maps onto $E/S$, a maximal overgroup $M$ of $CB_E^x$ in $E$ cannot contain $S$. Hence $M\cap S$ is proper in $S$ and contains the Borel subgroup $B_S^x$, so it is parabolic, a contradiction. So $E=CB_E^x$, a factorization of the almost simple group $E$ with solvable factor $B_E^x$. Since the image of $C$ in the semisimple factor is nontrivial and does not contain the socle, $C\not\geq S$ and $C$ is core-free in $E$ (Lemma \ref{lem:almost-simple-core-free}). Also, $B_E^x$ contains the Borel subgroup $B_S^x$ of $S$. We use the symplectic Li and Xia rows of Proposition \ref{prop:symplectic-no-p1-factorization}. For every $d\geq2$, the comparison at the characteristic prime between the solvable factor and a Borel subgroup of $S$ is $q^{d(d+1)/2}<q^{d^2}$. The finitely many special rows ($\operatorname{Sp}_6(2)$, $\operatorname{PSp}_6(3)$, and $\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$ for $q\in\{5,7,11,23\}$) satisfy the same comparison. Hence this comparison contradicts the factorization at every descent dimension. The one factorization case omitted from Proposition \ref{prop:symplectic-no-p1-factorization}, namely $(d,q)=(2,3)$ where $\operatorname{PSp}_4(3)\cong\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$, is handled directly. In this descent, for $u,v\in\ell^\perp$ the value $\langle u,v\rangle$ is unchanged by an element of the stabilizer of $\ell$ in the symplectic group. Therefore, this element acts on the symplectic quotient $\ell^\perp/\ell$ as an isometry with similitude factor $1$. No diagonal or conformal extension of the factor $S=\operatorname{PSp}_4(3)$ occurs in this descent. Although the lemma is stated for $E$ up to $\operatorname{PCSp}_4(3)$, only $E=S$ occurs in this descent. The symplectic factor of the Levi quotient of this line stabilizer is the simple socle itself, $E=S=\operatorname{PSp}_4(3)$. We have $C\leq S$, and Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction} makes $C$ hereditarily $S$-permutable, so Theorem \ref{thm:unitary} shows that $C=1$ or $C=S$, contrary to the hypothesis on $C$.

label: lem:symplectic-psp4-2-levi
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:symplectic-psp4-2-levi}
Let $C\leq S_6\cong\operatorname{PSp}_4(2)$ be a proper hereditarily $S_6$-permutable image occurring in the symplectic descent. Then either $C=A_6$, which is transitive on the fifteen totally singular planes of the natural $\mathbb{F}_2$ symplectic module of $\operatorname{PSp}_4(2)$, or $C$ fixes a totally singular line.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: If $C\leq A_6$, then $C$ is hereditarily $A_6$-permutable (Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction}), so $C\in\{1,A_6\}$ by the alternating theorem \cite{VT2012}. Since $S_6$ is transitive on the fifteen totally singular planes and the stabilizer $P_2$ in $S_6$ of a totally singular plane has order $48$ and contains odd permutations, $A_6P_2=S_6$. Consequently, the group $A_6$ is transitive on these planes. If instead $C\not\leq A_6$, then choose $b\in C\setminus A_6$. Let $K=C\cap A_6$. For $D\leq A_6$, hereditary $S_6$-permutability of $C$ provides $x\in\langle C,D\rangle$ with $CD^x=D^xC$. Replacing $x$ by $xb$ when $x\notin A_6$, we may take $x\in A_6$. Then $(CD^x)\cap A_6=KD^x$ is a subgroup. The subgroup $K$ is ordinary $A_6$-permutable (Lemma \ref{lem:normal-intersection-transfer}). Since $A_6\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(9)$, an ordinary $\operatorname{PSL}_2(9)$-permutable subgroup has order at most $2$ \cite[Theorem 1]{GT2025}, so $|K|\leq2$. As $C/K$ embeds in $S_6/A_6\cong C_2$, $|C|\leq4$. Then $C$ is a $2$-group, contained in a Sylow $2$-subgroup of $S_6\cong\operatorname{PSp}_4(2)$, the unipotent radical of a Borel subgroup of $\operatorname{PSp}_4(2)$, and so fixes a totally singular line.
head: environment

label: lem:symplectic-c2-borel-reduction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:symplectic-c2-borel-reduction}
For $q\geq4$, every proper hereditarily $\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$-permutable subgroup lies in a Borel subgroup of this symplectic group.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Let $A<\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$ be proper, nontrivial, and hereditarily $\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$-permutable. By Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} and Proposition \ref{prop:symplectic-no-p1-factorization}, we may assume that $A\leq P_1$. We obtain this conclusion by testing hereditary permutability of $A$ on the stabilizer $P_1$ in $\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$ of a totally isotropic line in its natural symplectic module. The Levi quotient of $P_1$ has rank one and acts projectively on $\ell^\perp/\ell$, where $\ell$ is the totally isotropic line fixed by $P_1$. A nontrivial proper image of $A$ in this quotient is settled by Lemma \ref{lem:pgl2-borel}. To show that the image of $A$ cannot be full, we test hereditary permutability of $A$ on the stabilizer $P_2$ of a totally singular plane. The argument in the case in which the semisimple image is full gives a contradiction. The trivial semisimple image of $A$ lies in $R_u(P_1)\rtimes\operatorname{GL}_1(q)$. We use Lemma \ref{lem:maximal-product} for $P_2$. The divisibility comparison between the index of $P_2$ and the order of $P_1$ in the case in which the semisimple image is full contradicts the product case. Hence $A\leq P_2^g$ for some $g$. Suppose that the singular line is not contained in the Lagrangian plane. The symplectic pairing between the singular line fixed by $P_1$ and the Lagrangian plane fixed by $P_2^g$ then induces a nonzero functional on the plane. The kernel of this functional is an $A$-stable singular line in the plane. Thus, whether or not the singular line fixed by $P_1$ lies in the Lagrangian plane fixed by $P_2^g$, these two subspaces determine a flag fixed by $A$. Hence $A$ lies in a Borel subgroup of $\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$.
head: environment

label: lem:symplectic-c2-borel
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:symplectic-c2-borel}
Let $S=\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)\leq E\leq\operatorname{PCSp}_4(q)$, and let $B_E$ be the normalizer in $E$ of a Borel subgroup of $S$. If $C\leq B_E$ is hereditarily $E$-permutable, then $C=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $q=2$, where $\operatorname{PSp}_4(2)\cong S_6$ is not simple, we enumerate in $\operatorname{Sp}_4(2)$ the subgroups of the Borel subgroup stabilizing the flag $\langle e_1\rangle<\langle e_1,e_2\rangle$. For each nontrivial subgroup $C$ in this enumeration, Appendix \ref{app:sp4-2-borel-certificate} gives a cyclic subgroup $H$ such that $CH^x\neq H^xC$ for every $x\in\langle C,H\rangle$. Consequently, every such $C$ fails the hereditary $E$-permutability condition, and the required conclusion $C=1$ holds. Assume that $q\geq3$. Take a root system of type $C_2$ \cite{Carter1985} with simple roots $\alpha$ (short) and $\beta$ (long). The positive roots are
$$
        \alpha,~\beta,~\alpha+\beta,~2\alpha+\beta.
$$
Let $B$ be the Borel subgroup of $S$ normalized by $B_E$. Let $T$ be a split maximal torus of $B$ and $U$ the subgroup generated by the four positive root subgroups. Then $B=UT$. Let $P_\alpha,P_\beta$ be the maximal parabolics of $E$ with Levi factors of rank one corresponding to $\alpha$ and $\beta$, respectively. Since $C\leq B_E\leq P_\alpha,P_\beta$, restriction from $E$ to these two parabolic subgroups (Lemma \ref{lem:overgroup-restriction}) makes $C$ hereditarily $P_\alpha$-permutable and hereditarily $P_\beta$-permutable. Next, apply inheritance of hereditary permutability by quotients (Lemma \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance}) to the respective Levi quotients of rank one of $P_\alpha$ and $P_\beta$. Consequently, the images of $C$ satisfy the hereditary permutability condition in their respective quotient groups. Moreover, each quotient lies between $\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ and $\operatorname{PGL}_2(q)$, and the image of $C$ lies in a Borel subgroup of that quotient. Since $q\geq3$, Lemma \ref{lem:pgl2-borel} shows that both images are trivial.

Hence the toral part of $C$ is trivial under $\alpha$ and $\beta$. Therefore, the toral part of $C$ is projectively central and hence trivial in $\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$. The $U_\alpha,U_\beta$ components of $C$ also vanish. Thus,
$$
        C\leq U_{\alpha+\beta}U_{2\alpha+\beta}.
$$
Conjugating $P_\beta$ by $s_\alpha$ gives a conjugate parabolic whose Levi factor has rank one. A root of this Levi factor is $s_\alpha(\beta)=2\alpha+\beta$. Therefore, inheritance of hereditary permutability by quotients, together with Lemma \ref{lem:pgl2-borel}, shows that the $U_{2\alpha+\beta}$ component of $C$ is trivial. Similarly, conjugating $P_\alpha$ by $s_\beta$ produces $s_\beta(\alpha)=\alpha+\beta$ and shows that the $U_{\alpha+\beta}$ component of $C$ is trivial. Hence $C=1$.

label: thm:symplectic-borel
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:symplectic-borel}
Let $S=\operatorname{PSp}_{2m}(q)\leq\widehat E\leq\operatorname{PCSp}_{2m}(q)$ with $m\geq2$, and let $B_{\widehat E}$ be the normalizer in $\widehat E$ of a Borel subgroup $B_S$ of $S$. If $C\leq B_{\widehat E}$ is hereditarily $\widehat E$-permutable, then $C=1$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
We induct on $m$. For $m=2$, we use Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-c2-borel}. Assume that $m\geq3$ and take a hyperbolic basis $e_1,\ldots,e_m,f_m,\ldots,f_1$ of the natural symplectic module of $S$, with $E_0=\langle e_1,\ldots,e_m\rangle$ the Lagrangian subspace whose complete flag is stabilized by $B_S$. This flag is $0=L_0<L_1<\cdots<L_m=E_0$, with $\dim L_i=i$ for $0\leq i\leq m$. The vectors $e_1,\ldots,e_m$ are chosen so that $L_i=\langle e_1,\ldots,e_i\rangle$ for $1\leq i\leq m$. Each $L_i$ is totally isotropic, and the last space $E_0$ is Lagrangian.

We consider the projective action of the stabilizer of $E_0$ in $\widehat E$ on $E_0$, and quotient that stabilizer by the elements acting as scalars on $E_0$. Write $P_{E_0}$ for this stabilizer and $\rho_0:P_{E_0}\to\operatorname{PGL}(E_0)$ for its projective action. The quotient is $P_{E_0}/\ker\rho_0$, identified with $\rho_0(P_{E_0})$. This quotient is linear, of socle $\operatorname{PSL}_m(q)$, between $\operatorname{PSL}_m(q)$ and $\operatorname{PGL}_m(q)$ \cite[Proposition 26.1(b)]{MalleTesterman2011}. The image of $C$ lies in a Borel subgroup of this Levi quotient. Therefore, Lemma \ref{lem:sl-borel} shows that this image of $C$ is trivial. In particular, the group $C$ acts projectively trivially on $E_0$. Hence all components corresponding to the roots $e_i-e_j$ vanish and all toral ratios on the $e_i$ are trivial. The common toral value is considered through the images of the projective symplectic actions on the spaces $W_i$.

For each $i$ let $W_i=\langle e_i\rangle^\perp/\langle e_i\rangle$. Consider the stabilizer in $\widehat E$ of $\langle e_i\rangle$ and its symplectic quotient on $W_i$. Denote this stabilizer by $P_i$ and its projective action on $W_i$ by $\rho_i$. We identify the quotient $P_i/\ker\rho_i$ with $\rho_i(P_i)$. Applying Lemma \ref{lem:quotient-inheritance} to this quotient shows that $\rho_i(C)$ is hereditarily $\rho_i(P_i)$-permutable. Moreover, it lies in the induced Borel subgroup of this quotient and hence is trivial by induction. The remaining positive roots are $e_a+e_b$ ($a<b$) and $2e_a$. Since $m\geq3$, each of these remaining positive roots occurs in the root system of the symplectic group on some $W_i$ ($i\notin\{a,b\}$ for $e_a+e_b$, and $i\neq a$ for $2e_a$). Hence all remaining unipotent components of $C$ vanish. The images of the projective symplectic actions on the spaces $W_i$ also force the toral characters corresponding to long roots to be trivial. So the toral part of $C$ is projectively central, hence trivial in $S$, and $C=1$.

label: prop:symplectic-psp4
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:symplectic-psp4}
For the simple group $G=\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$ there is no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: The case $q=2$ is not simple. For $q=3$, $\operatorname{PSp}_4(3)\cong\operatorname{PSU}_4(2)$ \cite[\S3.6.5]{Wilson2009} is covered by Theorem \ref{thm:unitary}. For $q\geq4$, Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-c2-borel-reduction} shows that every proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup is contained in a Borel subgroup of $G$. In this range, Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-c2-borel} shows that such a subgroup is trivial.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: For $m=1$, $\operatorname{PSp}_2(q)\cong\operatorname{PSL}_2(q)$ is simple only for $q\geq4$ and is then the known base case of Theorem \ref{thm:unitary-low-bases}. For $m=2$, use Proposition \ref{prop:symplectic-psp4}. Assume that $m\geq3$ and let $A<G$ be proper, nontrivial, and hereditarily $G$-permutable. The $P_1$-factorization case $G = AP_1 ^x$ is impossible (Proposition \ref{prop:symplectic-no-p1-factorization}), so $A\leq P_1$ after conjugating $A$ in $G$. The alternatives for the image of $A$ in the Levi quotient of $P_1$ (Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-actual-levi-alternatives}) lead to descent unless the semisimple image of $A$ is full or trivial. When the semisimple image of $A$ is full, suppose that $A$ were contained in $P_1\cap P_2^y$. Then the image of $A$ in the Levi quotient of $P_1$ would lie in a proper parabolic of that Levi quotient and could not be full. Therefore, $A$ can lie in no conjugate of the stabilizer $P_2$ in $G$ of a totally singular plane. By hereditary permutability of $A$ and maximality of the stabilizer $P_2$ of a totally singular plane, we have a factorization $G=AP_2^y$ with $|G:P_2|\mid|A|$. Analysing the index of $P_2$ in $G$ contradicts this factorization. If the semisimple image of $A$ is trivial, then $A$ lies in the inverse image in $P_1$ of the central torus of dimension one in its Levi quotient. This inverse image is $R_u(P_1)$ extended by this torus. We then use Theorem \ref{thm:symplectic-borel}. Repeating this descent through Levi quotients lowers the symplectic rank to the base $\operatorname{PSp}_4(q)$. For $q\geq3$ this is Proposition \ref{prop:symplectic-psp4}. By contrast, for $q=2$ the Levi factor $\operatorname{PSp}_4(2)\cong S_6$ is not simple, so Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-actual-levi-alternatives} cannot be used. Instead, Lemma \ref{lem:symplectic-psp4-2-levi} shows that the proper hereditarily $S_6$-permutable image $C$ of $A$ is either $A_6$ or fixes a singular line. When $C=A_6$, the image is transitive on the totally singular planes, so $A$ lies in no conjugate of $P_2$. As in the case of a full semisimple image, the comparison with the index of $P_2$ contradicts this possibility. When the image fixes a singular line, we extend the flag and the rank drops. When the image $C$ of $A$ in $S_6$ is trivial, $A$ lies in the inverse image of a Borel subgroup under the quotient map from the singular line stabilizer used at this descent step to its Levi quotient $\operatorname{PSp}_4(2)\cong S_6$. In this case, $A$ is trivial by Theorem \ref{thm:symplectic-borel}. The $m=2$ base of that theorem covers $q=2$ via Appendix \ref{app:sp4-2-borel-certificate}. So $A=1$, a contradiction.

label: thm:orthogonal
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:orthogonal}
For every simple projective orthogonal group $G=\mathrm{P}\Omega(V)$ there is no proper nontrivial hereditarily $G$-permutable subgroup.
head: environment

label: prop:orthogonal-no-p1-factorization
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:orthogonal-no-p1-factorization}
With $P_1$ the stabilizer of a singular line in $G$, the equality $G=AP_1^x$ cannot hold.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that $G=AP_1^x$. A proper parabolic of $G$ stabilizes a flag $0<U_1<\cdots<U_t$ of nonzero totally singular subspaces \cite[Table 3.5.B]{KleidmanLiebeck1990}, \cite[Proposition 26.1(b)]{MalleTesterman2011}. Therefore, this parabolic subgroup maps the set of singular lines contained in $U_1$ to itself. This set is a proper subset of the singular lines of $V$. Hence $A$ lies in no proper parabolic of $G$. By testing hereditary $G$-permutability of $A$ with a Borel subgroup $B$ of $G$, we have $B^y$ with $AB^y$ a subgroup. If $AB^y<G$, then a maximal subgroup of $G$ containing $AB^y$ contains the Borel subgroup $B^y$ and is parabolic, a contradiction. So $G=AB^y$, and for a maximal subgroup $M\geq A$ of $G$, the product $G=MB^y$ is a factorization with solvable factor $B^y$, which is covered by the classification of Li and Xia \cite{LiXia2022}.

For the orthogonal factorization $G=MB^y$, the Li and Xia rows are Table 1.1, rows 7--9, and Table 1.2, rows 22--28. We list the solvable factor and compare its $p$-part with the $p$-part of a Borel subgroup of the orthogonal socle $G$ in that row.

The factor $|m|_p$ or $|4|_p$ in the infinite rows comes from the permutation part of the table. label: lem:orthogonal-actual-levi-alternatives
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:orthogonal-actual-levi-alternatives}
With $W$ and $P_1$ as defined at the start of this subsection, let $S=\mathrm{P}\Omega(W)$ be the orthogonal socle of the Levi quotient of the singular line stabilizer $P_1$. Let $E$ be the image of the projective action of $P_1$ on $W$. This projective Levi quotient includes the diagonal factors and contains $S$. Let $C\leq E$ be hereditarily $E$-permutable. Then one of the following holds.
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}]
\item $C\geq S$.
\item $C$ has trivial image in the orthogonal socle $S$.
\item $C$ lies in the normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic subgroup of $S$.
\end{enumerate}
Suppose that $C$ lies in the normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic subgroup of $S$. In case {\rm (3)}, taking the inverse image in $P_1$ of this proper parabolic subgroup of $S$ extends the singular flag in $V$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md: Suppose that $C\not\geq S$, $C$ has nontrivial image in the orthogonal socle $S$, and $C$ does not lie in the normalizer in $E$ of a proper parabolic of $S$. We let $B_S$ be a Borel subgroup of $S$, and $B_E=N_E(B_S)$. The quotient $E/S$ corresponding to the diagonal part comes from a torus of the Levi quotient of $P_1$, so is represented by elements normalizing $B_S$ \cite[Example 24.22, Theorem 24.24]{MalleTesterman2011}, \cite[Proposition 26.1(b)]{MalleTesterman2011}. Therefore, the group $B_E$ maps onto $E/S$ and is solvable (an extension of $B_S$ by a toral quotient). By hereditary $E$-permutability of $C$, we have $B_E^x$ with $CB_E^x$ a subgroup. If $CB_E^x<E$, then a maximal subgroup $M$ of $E$ containing $CB_E^x$ cannot contain $S$. Then $M\cap S$ is proper and contains $B_S^x$, so it is parabolic in $S$. Hence $M\leq N_E(M\cap S)$, a contradiction. So $E=CB_E^x$, a factorization with solvable factor $B_E^x$ and a core-free subgroup $C$ of $E$ (Lemma \ref{lem:almost-simple-core-free}), with $B_E^x\cap S$ containing $B_S^x$. The orthogonal Li and Xia comparison \cite{LiXia2022} of Proposition \ref{prop:orthogonal-no-p1-factorization} contradicts this factorization. Finally, a proper parabolic of $\mathrm{P}\Omega(W)$ stabilizes a flag of nonzero totally singular subspaces in $W$. The quotient map is $p_\ell:\ell^\perp\to W$, given by $p_\ell(v)=v+\ell$. Consequently, the inverse image of this flag in $\ell^\perp$ under the quotient map onto $W$ is a totally singular flag in $V$ containing $\ell$, extending the singular flag.
head: environment

label: lem:orthogonal-full-levi-obstruction
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:orthogonal-full-levi-obstruction}
The case in which the image of $A$ contains the full orthogonal socle on $W=\ell^\perp/\ell$ cannot occur.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Suppose that the image of $A$ on $W$ contains $\mathrm{P}\Omega(W)$. By Witt's lemma \cite[Proposition 2.1.6]{KleidmanLiebeck1990}, the orthogonal group of $W$ is transitive on singular subspaces of a fixed dimension and type. Hence the image of $A$ stabilizes no nonzero proper totally singular subspace of $W$. Let $P_2$ be the stabilizer in $G$ of a totally singular plane of $V$, a maximal parabolic of $G$ \cite[Proposition 26.1(b)]{MalleTesterman2011}. By hereditary $G$-permutability of $A$ and Lemma ef{lem:maximal-product}, we have $A\leq P_2^g$ or $G=AP_2^g$.

If $A\leq P_2^g$, then let $Y$ be the totally singular plane of $V$ fixed by $P_2^g$. Since $A\leq P_1$ also fixes $\ell$ and $\ell^\perp$, we consider the positions of $Y$ relative to $\ell$ and $\ell^\perp$. If $\ell\leq Y$, then $Y/\ell$ is a singular line of $W$ fixed by the image of $A$ on $W$. If $\ell
ot\leq Y\leq\ell^\perp$, then the image of $Y$ in $W$ is a totally singular subspace fixed by the image of $A$ on $W$. If $Y
ot\leq\ell^\perp$, then $Y\cap\ell^\perp$ is an $A$-stable singular line $
eq\ell$, and $((Y\cap\ell^\perp)+\ell)/\ell$ is a singular line of $W$. Each position contradicts the hypothesis that the image of $A$ contains $\mathrm{P}\Omega(W)$. In the product case, $G=AP_2^g$ makes $A$ transitive on totally singular planes, but $A\leq P_1$ fixes $\ell$ and maps the family of totally singular planes containing $\ell$ to itself. Thus, $A$ is contained in no conjugate of $P_2$, and the factorization $G=AP_2^g$ is also impossible.
